passages.title: The Courtyard After Sunset
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Most visitors leave the courtyard garden when the library closes, but a second shift begins among the plants. At dusk, evening primrose opens pale flowers, and moths follow their scent through the dim air. Many moths feed on nectar with a long mouthpart while brushing against pollen. Some carry that pollen to the next flower they visit, helping the plants reproduce.

The garden offers more than blossoms. Dense stems give small insects shelter from wind, while fallen leaves protect damp ground where worms and other decomposers work. Meanwhile, a shallow dish of stones holds water without creating a deep pool. Caretakers rinse it and refill it, so insects can land on the stones. They also aim lamps away from the flower beds, because bright light can disrupt the movements of night-flying insects.

By morning, the moths are hidden, the primrose flowers are fading, and daytime visitors see only a tidy patch of green. Yet the courtyard has supported a whole round of feeding, pollination, and shelter during the hours when few people were watching.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A library courtyard needs bright lamps so visitors can study plants after closing.
Evening primrose is the only flower that can feed moths in a city garden.
A modest courtyard garden supports active nighttime life through flowers, shelter, water, and thoughtful care.
Garden caretakers should remove fallen leaves each morning to keep insects away.
questions.explanation: The passage follows the courtyard after people leave and shows several resources that support moths, insects, and decomposers through the night.

questions.stem: Why do the caretakers aim lamps away from the flower beds?
choices: They want the pale flowers to close earlier.
They need the fallen leaves to remain damp.
They are saving the lamps for daytime visitors.
They want to avoid disturbing the normal activity of night-flying insects.
questions.explanation: The text says bright light can disrupt night-flying insects, so directing the lamps elsewhere protects the garden's nighttime activity.

questions.stem: In the passage, what are “decomposers”?
choices: Living things that help break down dead material
Flowers that open only in complete darkness
Stones placed in a dish to hold extra heat
Lamps designed to shine beneath fallen leaves
questions.explanation: The decomposers work in damp ground protected by fallen leaves, which identifies them as organisms involved in breaking down natural remains.

questions.stem: What happens in the courtyard at dusk?
choices: Daytime visitors refill the shallow water dish.
Evening primrose opens pale flowers that attract moths.
Worms carry pollen from one flower to another.
The moths hide and the primrose flowers begin fading.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states that at dusk the evening primrose opens and moths follow the flowers' scent.

lesson.strategy: Track the courtyard across three times: closing, night, and morning. List what the plants and caretakers provide, then connect each resource to the living thing that uses it.

signals.means: Marks the start of the garden's less visible nighttime activity.
Adds a second kind of support while insects use the plants.
Shifts to what daytime visitors see after the active night has ended.

vocab.inContext: sweet liquid in flowers that feeds visiting moths
organisms that break down fallen natural material
the transfer of pollen that helps flowers reproduce

skillTips.main-idea: Combine the nighttime visitors with all four supports: blossoms, stems, leaves, and careful maintenance.
skillTips.inference: For a caretaker's choice, locate the stated effect and reason backward from what the choice prevents.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the damp leaves and worms around “decomposers” to identify the natural process they perform.
skillTips.detail: Follow the time markers closely; dusk and morning describe opposite stages of the courtyard's cycle.

passages.title: A Library for Drills and Ladders
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On most days, a drill spends far more time on a shelf than in a hand. A tool library turns that idle capacity into a shared resource. Instead of buying an item for one repair, members borrow from a catalog of drills, clamps, ladders, gardening tools, and other durable equipment. The model can lower the cost of occasional projects while reducing the number of objects each household must store.

Sharing requires more organization than a friendly loan across a fence. Each tool receives an inventory number, a checkout record, and a clear return date. Before each loan, a volunteer may inspect the cord, blade, guard, or handle and remove damaged equipment from circulation. Borrowers can also receive basic operating guidance, although the library cannot replace the manual or the judgment needed for a particular job.

A modest membership fee or refundable deposit may support maintenance and encourage returns. As a result, the library is not simply a room full of donated objects. It is a system of records, inspection, cleaning, and repair that keeps those objects dependable. Its deeper value is social: a neighbor can attempt a careful project without needing a private workshop, and practical knowledge travels with the tool.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly explaining?
choices: Damaged tools should always be donated to a library instead of being repaired at home.
A private workshop is the only dependable place to learn how to use durable equipment.
Membership deposits are the main reason neighbors return borrowed tools on time.
A tool library combines shared equipment with records and maintenance to expand practical access.
questions.explanation: The passage presents both the benefit of shared tools and the organized checkout, inspection, and repair system that makes sharing dependable.

questions.stem: Why are inventory numbers and checkout records especially important in a tool library?
choices: They make responsibility traceable when many people use the same equipment.
They prove that every donated tool has the same financial value.
They remove the need for return dates and equipment inspections.
They show borrowers which household originally owned each tool.
questions.explanation: Because the tools circulate among many members, records connect each item to its condition, location, and expected return.

questions.stem: What does “circulation” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: The flow of air around a tool's motor
The movement of equipment through shared use
The printed number attached to an item
The money collected through membership fees
questions.explanation: The volunteer removes damaged equipment from circulation, meaning it is taken out of the pool moving between the library and borrowers.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what may help pay for maintenance?
choices: A charge for every page in the operating manual
The sale of all tools after a single repair
A modest membership fee or refundable deposit
A payment from the household that first owned the item
questions.explanation: The final paragraph directly says that a modest membership fee or refundable deposit may support maintenance.

lesson.strategy: Separate the passage into access and reliability. The first explains why sharing helps; the next two show the records, inspections, and funding that keep the shared collection usable.

signals.means: Introduces borrowing as the alternative to private ownership.
Signals the inspection step that protects later borrowers.
Draws the conclusion that the library is an organized system, not just storage.

vocab.inContext: a tracked collection in which each tool has a number
movement of tools between the library and borrowers
able to be returned after the borrowing conditions are met

skillTips.main-idea: Choose a gist broad enough to include lower access costs and the system that keeps equipment dependable.
skillTips.inference: Ask what problem appears only when one object passes through many hands; the records answer that problem.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read what happens to a damaged tool: it is removed from the shared flow until it can be dependable again.
skillTips.detail: For funding questions, return to the final paragraph and distinguish a fee or deposit from operating guidance.

passages.title: Why a Clay Jar Cools Water
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An unglazed clay jar can cool the water inside it without a motor or a block of ice. The explanation begins in the jar's porous wall. Tiny connected spaces let a small amount of water seep toward the outer surface. When water seeps through the clay, it spreads into a thin film exposed to the surrounding air.

Some molecules in that film move fast enough to escape as vapor. To escape, they take energy with them, leaving the remaining water and the jar slightly cooler. This transfer of energy is evaporative cooling, the same general process that makes damp skin feel cool in a breeze. Air movement helps by carrying away vapor near the surface, allowing more liquid water to evaporate.

The effect has limits. If the surrounding humidity is high, the air already contains abundant water vapor, so evaporation slows. Glaze also blocks the pores that make seepage possible. A very thick jar may move water too slowly, while a crack may release it too quickly. For that reason, potters must balance strength with porosity rather than simply making the wall as open as possible.

The jar does not manufacture cold; it exchanges a small amount of water for a loss of thermal energy. That distinction explains both its usefulness and its dependence on dry, moving air. A community workshop demonstrating the jar is therefore teaching material science, weather, and careful design through one quiet vessel.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: A porous clay jar cools its contents through evaporation, but its performance depends on the wall and surrounding air.
A clay jar stays cold because its thick wall permanently blocks heat from reaching the water.
Potters glaze water jars mainly to increase the amount of evaporation from the outer surface.
A community workshop can make clay jars colder by placing electric motors inside them.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the seepage-and-evaporation mechanism, then examines how humidity, airflow, glaze, and wall structure limit it.

questions.stem: Why would the jar usually cool better in dry, moving air than in still, humid air?
choices: Dry air makes the clay wall thicker while wind closes any cracks.
Dry, moving air can accept and carry away more vapor, allowing evaporation to continue.
Humid air pulls too much liquid through the clay before it can cool.
Still air changes the water molecules into glaze on the jar's surface.
questions.explanation: The text says humidity slows evaporation and airflow carries vapor away, so dry movement preserves the conditions for energy-removing evaporation.

questions.stem: In this passage, what does “porosity” refer to?
choices: The amount of water stored in the center of a jar
The strength of the breeze moving past a vessel
The degree to which a material contains tiny connected openings
The temperature at which liquid changes into solid clay
questions.explanation: The porous wall contains connected spaces that let water seep outward, so porosity describes the presence and openness of those passages.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does glaze do to the cooling process?
choices: It makes surrounding air less humid.
It increases the speed of molecules in the water.
It strengthens airflow along the outer surface.
It blocks the pores needed for water to seep outward.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explicitly states that glaze blocks the pores that make seepage, and therefore evaporation, possible.

lesson.strategy: Build a four-link chain: pores allow seepage, seepage makes a film, evaporation removes energy, and the remaining water cools. Then test each limit against one link in that chain.

signals.means: Begins the physical sequence at the jar's outer surface.
Explains why departing water molecules remove energy.
Connects competing material limits to the potter's design balance.

vocab.inContext: containing tiny connected spaces through which water can seep
the amount of water vapor already present in the air
related to heat energy lost as some water evaporates

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the cooling mechanism and its limits; a choice about evaporation alone leaves out the design problem.
skillTips.inference: Combine two statements from different paragraphs: humidity fills the air with vapor, while movement carries vapor away.
skillTips.vocabulary: Return to the tiny connected spaces in the first paragraph to define “porosity” through visible structure.
skillTips.detail: Keep pores and glaze in opposition: pores permit seepage, while glaze seals the route the water would take.

passages.title: Garrett Morgan's Safer Signal
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Garrett Morgan was born in Kentucky in 1877. As a young man, he moved to Cleveland and learned to repair sewing machines. He later opened his own shop and kept solving practical problems.

By the 1920s, city streets held cars, bicycles, wagons, and walkers. One day, Morgan saw a crash at an intersection. He began thinking about a safer signal. Existing signals often moved directly between stop and go. Morgan designed a three-position device with a pause that stopped traffic in every direction. This short break let an intersection clear before traffic started again.

In 1923, Morgan received a patent for his design. His hand-operated signal was not the same as every modern traffic light. Still, its extra interval showed how a small change could make a shared street safer. Morgan saw an ordinary public object and found room to improve it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of this biography?
choices: Garrett Morgan became successful by building modern electric traffic lights in Kentucky.
Garrett Morgan used practical skill to add a safer pause to an early traffic signal.
City streets stopped using wagons as soon as Morgan moved to Cleveland.
Repairing sewing machines was Morgan's only important work.
questions.explanation: The biography connects Morgan's practical repair experience to his signal with an all-direction pause that improved street safety.

questions.stem: What does Morgan's early work suggest about him?
choices: He avoided machines because they were too difficult to repair.
He planned to replace city streets with sewing shops.
He learned by working with machines and applying ideas to practical needs.
He believed useful inventions had to be large and electric.
questions.explanation: Morgan learned sewing-machine repair, opened a shop, and kept solving problems, which supports an image of hands-on learning and practical invention.

questions.stem: What does “patent” mean in this passage?
choices: A busy crossing used by cars and wagons
A machine that repairs torn cloth
A short pause when all traffic stops
An official right granted for an invention
questions.explanation: Morgan received the patent for his design, so the word refers to official recognition and rights connected to an invention.

questions.stem: In what year did Morgan receive his patent?
questions.explanation: The last paragraph begins by stating that Morgan received a patent for the signal design in 1923.

lesson.strategy: Read the biography as problem, experience, and improvement. Morgan's repair work shows his method; the street crash gives him a new problem; the added pause is his answer.

signals.means: Introduces the practical experience Morgan gained early in life.
Marks the street event that focused his attention on signals.
Gives the date when his signal design received a patent.

vocab.inContext: a place where streets and streams of traffic cross
the short all-stop period between other signals
an official right connected to Morgan's invention

skillTips.main-idea: Link Morgan's practical skill to the safer pause he added; neither the shop nor the crash is the whole biography.
skillTips.inference: Use the pattern of repairing, opening a shop, and solving problems to describe how Morgan learned and worked.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “for his design” shows that a patent is tied to an invention, not to a street or a machine part.
skillTips.detail: Dates play different roles: 1877 marks Morgan's birth, while 1923 marks the patent for the signal.

passages.title: The Cost of One More Potter
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A community pottery room has costs before anyone shapes a bowl. Before anyone arrives, the group must pay for rent, tables, shelves, and a kiln. These are fixed costs because they do not change much when one more member joins.

Other expenses grow with use. One more pot requires clay, glaze, kiln space, and some cleanup. Economists call the added expense a marginal cost. It is usually smaller than the full cost of operating the studio. That difference explains why sharing can make an expensive craft more affordable. Many members divide the fixed costs, while each person still covers the materials they use.

Yet the room has a limit. By contrast, the savings shrink after every worktable is taken. The group may need longer hours or another kiln firing. Once the room is full, the next member can cause a large jump in cost. Good pricing therefore considers both shared savings and capacity. A low fee may welcome members, but it must also keep the tables, tools, and kiln working well.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Every member of a pottery studio should own a personal kiln and worktable.
Clay and glaze are fixed costs because a studio buys them before opening.
A shared studio lowers costs by dividing fixed expenses, but limited capacity still affects pricing.
Community pottery rooms become cheaper each time they reach their space limit.
questions.explanation: The passage first shows how members share fixed costs, then explains why crowding and added capacity can make the next member more expensive.

questions.stem: Why might one new member become costly after the room is full?
choices: The existing members stop using clay and glaze.
Rent becomes a marginal cost for the first time.
The new member must build a private studio at home.
Serving that member may require more hours or an additional kiln firing.
questions.explanation: Once current space and time are fully used, the passage says another person may trigger a larger step such as extended hours or another firing.

questions.stem: What is a “marginal cost” in this passage?
choices: The added expense caused by making one more pot or serving one more member
The full price of opening and operating the entire studio
A fee that never changes when the studio becomes crowded
The value of a finished pot after it leaves the kiln
questions.explanation: The text defines marginal cost through the extra clay, glaze, kiln space, and cleanup required for one additional pot.

questions.stem: Which pair does the passage present as fixed costs?
choices: Glaze and cleanup
Rent and shelves
One pot and one kiln firing
Longer hours and clay
questions.explanation: Rent and shelves appear in the opening list of costs that exist before anyone arrives and change little with one more member.

lesson.strategy: Sort every studio expense into one of two columns: costs shared before work begins and costs added by more use. Then notice how a full room changes the second column.

signals.means: Identifies expenses that exist even before members use the studio.
Turns from the savings of sharing to the limit created by crowding.
Marks the point where one more member may require a costly expansion.

vocab.inContext: costs that change little when one more person joins
describing the expense added by one more unit of use
the amount of activity the room and equipment can handle

skillTips.main-idea: A complete gist needs both parts: shared fixed costs create savings, while full capacity can create new expense.
skillTips.inference: When the room is full, look for the next required resource; added hours and firings explain the cost jump.
skillTips.vocabulary: The sentence before the term lists what one more pot adds, giving a direct context definition of “marginal.”
skillTips.detail: Return to the opening list for fixed costs, and avoid choices that mix those items with clay or cleanup.

passages.title: The Noticeboard's Slow Conversation
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A cork noticeboard in a shared entryway cannot compete with a phone for speed. Its messages wait in one place: a request for garden pots, the date of a choir practice, a sketch of a missing glove. At first glance, this stillness seems like a weakness. News cannot chase anyone who walks past.

Yet the board offers a different kind of attention. Everyone who stops sees the same finite surface rather than a private stream chosen for them. A new card must fit beside older needs, so the crowded corners become a rough portrait of local priorities. Pinholes and faded rectangles also preserve a small memory of what the entryway has carried.

The board requires care. Someone must remove the expired concert notice, straighten the curling paper, and leave room for the next voice. That work is a form of editing, but it should not become control by the person holding the pins. That is why clear dates and simple posting rules matter. The noticeboard's value lies neither in speed nor permanence. It offers a slow, shared conversation that remains visible long enough for neighbors to encounter it together.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the essay's main idea?
choices: A noticeboard should display only one message at a time so the entryway stays visually empty.
Phone messages are slow because they remain fixed in one physical place.
The person holding the pins should control every idea posted in a shared entryway.
A cared-for noticeboard creates a slow, shared conversation by keeping local messages visible together.
questions.explanation: The essay contrasts speed with a finite public surface, then argues that simple care lets neighbors encounter local messages together.

questions.stem: Why are the pinholes and faded rectangles meaningful to the writer?
choices: They are traces of earlier messages and give the entryway a small public memory.
They prove that every old notice should remain posted forever.
They show that the board has never been used for local priorities.
They prevent new cards from fitting beside older needs.
questions.explanation: The text says those physical traces preserve a memory of what the entryway has carried, linking marks to earlier community messages.

questions.stem: What does “finite” mean as used to describe the board's surface?
choices: Visible only to the person who posted a card
Limited in size or amount
Able to update itself without human care
Reserved permanently for concert notices
questions.explanation: New cards must share a crowded surface with older needs, showing that “finite” means bounded rather than endless.

questions.stem: Which task does the passage identify as noticeboard care?
choices: Sending every message to a private phone stream
Saving each faded notice in its original position
Removing an expired notice and straightening curling paper
Covering old pinholes before anyone can see them
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names removing the expired concert notice and straightening curling paper as necessary care.

lesson.strategy: Compare speed with shared visibility. The board cannot chase readers, but its finite surface gathers local needs in one view; upkeep then determines whether that conversation stays open.

signals.means: Introduces the quick judgment that a board's stillness is merely a weakness.
Turns from the board's lack of speed to its shared form of attention.
Connects responsible editing with dates and fair posting rules.

vocab.inContext: limited to one physical surface shared by all the cards
local needs and events that receive space and attention
no longer current and ready to be removed from the board

skillTips.main-idea: Balance the board's limitation with its value: it is slow and bounded, yet public, shared, and locally revealing.
skillTips.inference: Treat marks on the cork as evidence of time; they matter because earlier notices leave a visible history behind.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the crowded corners and need to leave room for new cards to infer that “finite” means limited.
skillTips.detail: Find the maintenance verbs in the last paragraph: remove, straighten, and leave room all describe care.

passages.title: The Peacock and the Well Rope
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before the spring feast, Peacock decided that the village well looked too plain. She braided a garland of leaves and bright petals around its posts, then polished the bucket until the wood shone. Mole noticed that the rope was frayed where it crossed the stone rim. He brought a new coil and began measuring, knotting, and testing it.

While Peacock worked, she drew a cheerful crowd. The animals admired how the petals fluttered and how their faces gleamed in the bucket's metal bands. Nearby, Mole fastened the replacement rope and pulled up three heavy buckets. Hardly anyone watched him lower each one again to check the strain.

When the cooks arrived, they needed water for the feast. Peacock's garland made the well inviting, but Mole's rope carried bucket after bucket without slipping. Then a sharp wind swept across the square and scattered most of the petals. The polished bucket still shone, and the water kept rising.

Peacock first mourned the empty posts. Then she saw the cooks filling their pots and understood which work the feast depended upon. The next morning, she asked Mole to show her how to spot worn fibers. At the following feast, the well was again beautiful, but Peacock checked the rope before she gathered a single flower.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: Visible beauty can welcome people, but dependable care must come before decoration.
A village should decorate its well only when no feast is planned.
Mole proves that flowers have no useful place in a shared square.
Peacock learns that polished buckets should never be used to carry water.
questions.explanation: The garland adds welcome, but the feast relies on Mole's sound rope; Peacock finally combines beauty with checking the essential structure first.

questions.stem: Why does Mole lift and lower three heavy buckets?
choices: He wants the crowd to admire his strength instead of Peacock's flowers.
He is testing whether the new rope and knots can bear repeated weight.
He needs to wash the petals from the well before the cooks arrive.
He hopes the bucket's metal bands will polish the stone rim.
questions.explanation: The repeated heavy lifts occur just after Mole fastens the rope, and the text says he checks the strain, so they are a load test.

questions.stem: What does “frayed” mean as used to describe the rope?
choices: Newly braided with leaves and petals
Hidden beneath a smooth metal cover
Worn so that some fibers are coming apart
Pulled tight enough to lift three buckets
questions.explanation: Mole replaces the rope and later teaches Peacock to spot worn fibers, showing that “frayed” means worn and beginning to separate.

questions.stem: What scatters most of Peacock's petals?
choices: Water spilling from the cooks' pots
The bucket rubbing against the garland
Mole carrying the new coil across the square
A sharp wind
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that a sharp wind sweeps across the square and scatters most of the petals.

lesson.strategy: Compare the two kinds of work at the well. Peacock improves what visitors see, while Mole strengthens what bears weight. The feast reveals which task is essential and how both can coexist.

signals.means: Sets up the preparation period when both animals choose their tasks.
Opens a contrast between public attention and Mole's quiet testing.
Begins the practical test that reveals what the feast truly needs.

vocab.inContext: a decorative chain of leaves and bright petals
worn at the rim so that the rope's fibers were separating
the force placed on the rope by a heavy bucket

skillTips.main-idea: Do not reject beauty entirely; the ending keeps the well beautiful but places the rope inspection first.
skillTips.inference: Connect Mole's repeated lifts to the later demand for many buckets; he is checking the rope under real strain.
skillTips.vocabulary: The replacement rope and the later reference to worn fibers define what happened to the old, frayed rope.
skillTips.detail: Separate what the wind changes from what remains: petals scatter, while the rope, bucket, and water service continue.

passages.title: The Path Made by Many Feet
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A dirt path crosses the corner of a public green. No planner drew it, and no single walker made it. One person first stepped off the paved route to shorten a trip. Others followed the faint line, pressed the grass, and gradually produced a path that now guides strangers who never met its makers.

Who, then, is the path's author? Giving credit to the first walker ignores the many feet needed to keep the line visible. Giving equal credit to everyone ignores differences: some opened the route, some strengthened it, and most merely accepted an invitation already present. Authorship here is distributed across unequal contributions, none of which is sufficient alone.

The same puzzle appears in responsibility. If rain cuts a rut into the path, each walker can say that one footstep caused almost nothing. Even so, the combined traffic may damage the green or reveal where a paved connection is genuinely needed. A city that simply blocks the path treats collective behavior as an error. A city that immediately formalizes it may overlook drainage, wildlife, or access needs that the shortcut does not solve.

The deeper lesson is that a shared result can be real even when no participant intended the whole. Collective authorship does not remove individual judgment, but it changes its scale. We should ask not only, What did my step do? We should also ask, What pattern am I joining, and what stewardship does that pattern now require?

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage's main idea?
choices: Every informal path should be paved as soon as walkers begin using it.
Shared outcomes complicate authorship and responsibility because many unequal actions can create one real pattern.
The first person to leave a paved route owns any path that later appears.
Individual choices become morally unimportant whenever many people make them.
questions.explanation: The path illustrates both distributed authorship and shared responsibility, with the closing questions shifting attention from one step to the pattern.

questions.stem: Why does the author reject both automatically blocking and automatically paving the path?
choices: Either response would give the first walker too much legal credit.
Both responses would prevent rain from making a rut in the green.
The path provides useful evidence, but it does not reveal every need or consequence by itself.
A public green cannot contain both a paved route and an informal shortcut.
questions.explanation: The shortcut may reveal demand, yet the text names drainage, wildlife, and access concerns it cannot settle, so its message requires judgment.

questions.stem: What does “stewardship” most nearly mean in the final sentence?
choices: The right to claim sole credit for a public path
The habit of choosing the shortest available route
The process of measuring the length of a footstep
Responsible care for something affected or shared
questions.explanation: The final question asks what the joined pattern now requires, so stewardship means accepting responsibility for the shared result and its effects.

questions.stem: How does the passage say the informal path gradually becomes visible?
choices: Walkers follow a faint line and press the grass.
A planner marks the route with painted stones.
Rain fills a trench dug by the first walker.
The city removes the paved route beside it.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says later walkers follow the faint line and press the grass, gradually producing the path.

lesson.strategy: Use the path as a model rather than the final topic. First trace who creates it, then transfer that distributed pattern to responsibility, policy, and the closing question about care.

signals.means: Turns the physical path into a question about distributed authorship.
Counters the tiny effect of one step with the real effect of combined traffic.
Moves from the park example to the passage's general philosophical claim.

vocab.inContext: credit for creating a path that no one walker made alone
turns the informal shortcut into an officially designed route
responsible care for the shared pattern and its consequences

skillTips.main-idea: Your gist must join two questions—who made the path and who should care for its effects—under one collective pattern.
skillTips.inference: Treat the shortcut as evidence, not a complete plan; then notice the other concerns that evidence leaves unanswered.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read “require” beside “stewardship”; the word names a duty of care created by joining the pattern.
skillTips.detail: Keep the path's stages in order: one walker leaves pavement, others follow, and repeated pressure makes the line visible.

passages.title: When the Hall Goes Quiet
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A community hall has an old fan that makes a soft hum. New visitors notice it at once. At first, the sound may seem loud. After a while, regular visitors stop hearing it unless they choose to listen.

This change is called habituation. The brain pays less attention to a steady signal that brings no new information. That leaves more attention for voices, work, or music in the room. The ears still receive the sound, but the mind treats it as background.

When the fan stops, people often look up. The sudden quiet is a change, so attention returns. The same pattern can happen with a clock's tick or the smell of a familiar room. Habituation helps us avoid reacting to every steady detail. It also explains why a visitor may notice something that regular users miss.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Old fans always make more noise than clocks and music.
Regular visitors hear every sound more clearly than new visitors do.
Habituation reduces attention to steady input, while a change can make attention return.
A quiet room prevents the brain from noticing voices or work.
questions.explanation: The fan example shows attention fading when a sound stays steady and returning when the familiar hum suddenly stops.

questions.stem: Why may a new visitor notice the fan more than a regular visitor?
choices: The fan becomes louder whenever a new person enters.
Regular visitors can no longer hear any sound in the hall.

passages.title: Why the Heavy Door Closes Gently
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A heavy public door may swing open easily and then close without slamming. The small box above it is a door closer. Inside, a spring and a chamber of oil work together.

When you pull the door open, an arm turns a shaft and squeezes the spring. The spring stores energy. Once you let go, that energy pushes the door back toward its frame. A spring alone would move too quickly. Instead of letting it snap shut, the closer forces oil through a narrow valve. The restricted flow slows the arm and controls the door's speed.

Near the end of the swing, a separate adjustment may let the door move firmly enough to reach the latch. The settings must balance several needs. The door should give a person time to pass, resist a hard slam, and still close fully. A trained maintainer can adjust some closers for the door and setting. This quiet mechanism turns one pull into a controlled return, helping a shared entrance work again and again.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly explaining?
choices: Why every public door should remain open between visitors
How a latch stores the energy needed to open a heavy door
Why a door closer must be replaced after each strong pull
How a spring, oil, and adjustments make a door return at a controlled speed
questions.explanation: The passage follows energy into the spring, oil through the valve, and the final adjustment to explain one controlled closing cycle.

questions.stem: Why does the closer force oil through a narrow valve?
choices: The resistance slows the spring's return so the door does not snap shut.
The oil needs to reach the latch and glue the door closed.
The narrow valve makes the public door lighter to lift.
The oil must leave the closer before the spring can store energy.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts the fast motion of a spring alone with restricted oil flow, which slows the arm and controls speed.

questions.stem: What is the “latch” in this passage?
choices: The box that contains the spring and oil
The part that catches and holds the closed door
The shaft that turns when someone pulls
The narrow passage that restricts the oil
questions.explanation: The door must move firmly enough to reach the latch and close fully, identifying the latch as the part that catches the door.

choices: The frame
The valve
The spring
The latch
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly states that opening the door squeezes the spring and that the spring stores energy.

lesson.strategy: Trace one opening and closing cycle. A pull compresses the spring, release returns its energy, the valve slows that return, and the final adjustment helps the latch catch.

signals.means: Starts the sequence by showing how energy enters the spring.
Contrasts an uncontrolled snap with the oil-controlled motion.
Shifts attention to the final part of the swing and the latch.

vocab.inContext: a turning rod moved by the closer's outer arm
a narrow control point that slows the flow of oil
the part that catches the door when it reaches the frame

skillTips.main-idea: Include the complete mechanism rather than naming only the spring; oil and the final adjustment control its return.
skillTips.inference: Use the contrast with a spring alone to infer why restricted oil flow is useful: it prevents excess speed.
skillTips.vocabulary: The clues “reach” and “close fully” show that the latch is the catching point at the end of motion.
skillTips.detail: Keep each part's job separate: the spring stores, the valve slows, and the latch catches.

passages.title: The Closet Map
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On Monday, Lian became keeper of a neighborhood hall's supply closet. She counted every roll of tape, extension cord, paintbrush, and broom. Then she placed each item where it seemed logical and labeled the shelves.

By Wednesday, the closet was tidy and useless. The dance group could not find floor tape because Lian had filed it with office supplies. Gardeners left muddy gloves on a chair because their shelf was too high. Lian spent the evening returning objects to places that made sense only to her.

The next morning, she removed every label. She asked each arriving group to find and return its usual supplies. She watched where their hands reached first. Then she traced an outline behind each hanging tool, moved common items to the middle shelves, and used labels chosen by the people who shared the closet.

During the festival, a paper banner tore just before the doors opened. A volunteer ran to the closet and returned with tape in seconds. Lian heard the quick repair but no praise for the shelves. She smiled anyway. A good map, she realized, becomes almost invisible when it matches the way people actually move.

choices: Lian turns a failed organizing system into a useful one by observing how other people actually use the closet.

The dance group and gardeners compete to control the neighborhood hall.
A tidy closet is useful only when its keeper receives public praise.
questions.explanation: Lian's first system reflects only her logic; after observing users and revising the layout, a volunteer finds tape immediately during a real need.

questions.stem: Why does Lian smile even though nobody praises the shelves?
choices: She plans to hide the tape again after the festival.
The quick, unnoticed repair proves that the new system works naturally.
She thinks the torn banner looks better without tape.
The groups have agreed that labels are never useful.
questions.explanation: The volunteer finds tape in seconds, fulfilling Lian's goal; the lack of comment shows the system has become effortless rather than unappreciated.

questions.stem: What does “logical” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: Too high for anyone to reach
Marked by an outline on the wall
Reasonable according to an organized way of thinking
Chosen by every group using the hall
questions.explanation: Lian's first placements follow an orderly system that makes sense to her, even though the later confusion shows it does not fit other users.

An extension cord

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that the volunteer returns from the closet with tape and makes the quick repair.

lesson.strategy: Track Lian's definition of order through three tests: her own neat layout, other groups' confusion, and the festival repair. The outcome shows why observation changes her method.

skillTips.main-idea: A full gist needs the failure and the revision; simply saying Lian tidies a closet misses what she learns from users.
skillTips.inference: Use the fast repair as the evidence behind Lian's smile; success is measured in finding tape, not receiving praise.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast what seems “logical” to Lian with what works for the groups to separate orderly thought from shared usability.
skillTips.detail: The final problem is narrow: a paper banner tears, and tape is the item that returns from the closet.

passages.title: Bread Day at the Terrace Oven
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In some nineteenth-century Welsh industrial settlements, a row of homes shared a large bread oven. Many small houses lacked an oven able to bake enough loaves for a household. Building a separate large oven for every family would also have demanded space and fuel. A communal bakehouse concentrated the heat in one sturdy structure.

At terrace communities near ironworks, families often prepared dough at home and carried it to the shared oven. Some ovens followed a schedule that gave each household a baking day. Elsewhere, an appointed baker tended the fire and charged a small fee for each loaf. Because the oven held many loaves, one firing could serve several homes.

The arrangement required coordination. Dough had to be ready when the oven was hot, and loaves or tins needed to remain identifiable. The person tending the oven judged heat without a precise thermometer, using practiced attention to the fire, masonry, and bread. Baking day therefore joined domestic skill to a shared timetable.

Over time, household ranges and commercial bakeries became more common, and many communal ovens disappeared. Their surviving structures show that everyday infrastructure was once organized differently. The oven did more than bake bread: it divided scarce heat across neighbors, turned timing into a civic routine, and made one building part of many kitchens.

Communal ovens let neighboring households share heat, equipment, and a coordinated baking routine.
Every industrial settlement used one identical schedule and charged the same fee per loaf.

questions.explanation: The passage explains why one oven served many homes, how schedules or bakers coordinated it, and what the arrangement reveals about shared infrastructure.

choices: Families were not allowed to prepare their own dough at home.
Each loaf needed a separate building and a separate fire.
Several households had to match their prepared dough to the period when one shared oven was hot.
Commercial bakeries delivered all loaves at a fixed hour.
questions.explanation: One firing served several homes, so households needed to coordinate their dough and turns with a shared period of usable heat.

questions.stem: What does “infrastructure” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: A recipe passed from one household to another
The practiced skill of judging bread by sight
A fee paid to a person who tends a fire

questions.explanation: The surviving oven is a shared structure that supports the daily work of many kitchens, so it is an example of community infrastructure.

questions.stem: What two methods of organizing oven use does the passage describe?
choices: A household baking schedule or an appointed baker charging by the loaf

questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes assigned baking days in some places and a paid, appointed baker in others.

lesson.strategy: Read the oven as both a building and a schedule. Identify the physical resources it combines, then trace the timing, labor, and identification needed when many kitchens share one heat source.

skillTips.inference: Think of oven heat as a limited window: prepared dough from several homes had to arrive while that window was open.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “one building part of many kitchens” provides a concrete example of what infrastructure supports.
skillTips.detail: The passage offers two alternatives, not one universal custom: scheduled household days or an appointed paid baker.

passages.title: Why the Park Keeps a Fallen Log
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In a managed park, a fallen trunk can look like unfinished work. Visitors may see clutter, while a caretaker sees a question: is the wood blocking a path or creating useful habitat? To a hurried eye, removing every fallen limb seems like the tidiest form of care. Ecology makes the decision less simple.

A log begins changing as soon as fungi and bacteria enter its tissues. Beetle larvae and other small animals open passages, while mosses may hold moisture at the surface. As decay advances, the wood softens and creates a microhabitat with different shade, dampness, and temperature from the open ground. Small animals can shelter in its cracks, and decomposers gradually return nutrients to the surrounding soil.

Not every dead tree should remain exactly where it falls. A trunk across a walkway, a dangerously suspended branch, or wood near vulnerable structures may require removal or relocation. Yet a section placed away from heavy foot traffic can keep ecological value without creating the same obstruction. Some caretakers also retain part of a standing dead trunk when a careful assessment shows that it can be left appropriately.

For a park keeper, then, tidiness is not the only measure of good maintenance. The goal is not neglect, but selective care: distinguish hazards from habitat, preserve useful structure where conditions allow, and explain why a weathered log may belong in a well-tended landscape.

choices: Park workers should leave every fallen tree untouched wherever it lands.
A tidy park contains no fungi, beetles, mosses, or decomposing material.

A fallen log provides useful habitat only after all of its wood has become soil.
questions.explanation: The passage balances the ecological roles of deadwood with reasons to move or remove it, defining maintenance as selective rather than absolute.

questions.stem: Why does the author say keeping some deadwood is not the same as neglect?
choices: Deadwood never creates an obstruction in a managed park.
Visitors always prefer logs to open ground and clear paths.
Fallen wood remains unchanged unless a caretaker moves it.
Caretakers can assess location and risk, then deliberately preserve useful habitat where conditions allow.
questions.explanation: The passage describes assessment, relocation, and hazard distinctions, showing that retained wood can result from an active management choice.

choices: A small local environment with its own shade, moisture, and temperature
A paved route designed to keep visitors away from wood
A suspended branch that must always be left standing
A method for measuring the age of a fallen tree
questions.explanation: The text defines the softened log's microhabitat through conditions that differ from open ground, including shade, dampness, and temperature.

choices: Moss holding moisture on a log's surface
A trunk lying across a walkway

questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists a trunk across a walkway among the conditions that may call for removal or relocation.

lesson.strategy: Make two columns labeled habitat and hazard. Add each role or location of deadwood to the right column, then use the final paragraph to see why selective care must consider both.

Signals how the log's structure and ecological uses change over time.

skillTips.inference: Look for active verbs such as assess, relocate, distinguish, and preserve to see why retention can be deliberate work.
skillTips.vocabulary: The clause after “microhabitat” supplies its dimensions: local shade, dampness, and temperature.
skillTips.detail: Separate ecological processes from placement problems; the walkway example is the direct obstruction.

passages.title: A Fair Lost-and-Found
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A good lost-and-found is more than a box under a desk. It uses a simple routine so an item can return to its owner.

First, a worker records where and when the object was found. A tag with that information stays with the object. Next, similar things are stored together, such as hats on one shelf and water bottles on another. Valuable items may be kept in a more secure place.

When someone makes a claim, the worker asks for details that were not shared publicly. A person might name the color inside a bag or the mark on a key ring. Those details help match the owner to the object. At closing time, the record shows what arrived, what was returned, and what remains. Clear records turn a pile of stray things into a fair system.

choices: Every lost object should be displayed in public with all its details.
A lost-and-found works best when valuable things are mixed with hats and bottles.
A worker can identify an owner by asking only where the object was found.
Records, organized storage, and private details help a lost-and-found return items fairly.
questions.explanation: The passage explains a complete routine: record the find, store it clearly, verify a claim with private details, and update the record.

questions.stem: Why are some details about a lost item not shared publicly?
choices: A true owner can use an unshared feature to show special knowledge of the item.
Workers do not have enough room to write details on a record.
The details would prevent similar objects from being stored together.
Public details make valuable objects too difficult to secure.
questions.explanation: The worker asks a claimant for an inside color or private mark, so matching an unshared detail helps distinguish the owner from a guesser.

questions.stem: What is a “claim” in the third paragraph?
choices: A label showing where an item is stored
A request stating that an item belongs to someone
A locked place for keeping valuable objects
A list of everything left at closing time
questions.explanation: The claim begins the process of matching a person to an object, so it is the person's request to receive something said to be theirs.

choices: Inside a bag
Under the desk
Together on one shelf
Beside the key rings
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives hats on one shelf as an example of storing similar objects together.

lesson.strategy: Follow one lost item through four stages: record, tag, storage, and claim. At each stage, ask how the step makes the final match more accurate or fair.

signals.means: Begins the routine with a record of the object's discovery.
Moves from recording the object to organizing its storage.
Marks the final check of what arrived, left, or remains.

skillTips.main-idea: Choose a gist that covers the whole return system, not just tags, shelves, valuables, or one example.
skillTips.inference: Ask how a worker can tell an owner from a guesser; an unshared feature provides the needed test.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use what follows the claim—the worker asks questions and matches owner to object—to define the request.
skillTips.detail: The storage examples are paired clearly: hats share one shelf, while water bottles share another.

passages.title: How Paste Joins Torn Paper
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At a paper-repair table, a thin paste can join torn fibers without hiding the page under thick glue. One traditional adhesive begins as wheat starch and water.

When the mixture warms, starch granules absorb water and swell. The cloudy liquid thickens into a smooth paste. A repairer brushes a small amount onto a strip of strong, thin paper and lays it across a tear. The wet paste reaches the tiny spaces among the paper fibers.

As it dries, water leaves the mixture. Starch molecules remain between the overlapping fibers and help hold the two papers together. Because the adhesive is water-based, a trained conservator can often soften it with controlled moisture if a repair later needs to be changed. That possibility is called reversibility.

The useful bond depends on care. Too much paste can stain or stiffen a sheet, and poor storage can spoil the mixture. In skilled hands, wheat starch paste provides a light, strong connection. Its science is quiet: water opens the structure, and drying leaves the adhesive behind.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly explaining?
choices: Warmed wheat starch forms a careful, potentially reversible bond as paste enters paper fibers and dries.
Paper repair works best when a thick layer of permanent glue hides the tear.
Dry starch granules can repair a page without water, warmth, or another strip of paper.
A conservator removes all fibers from a torn page before applying paste.
questions.explanation: The passage traces starch and water through warming, application, and drying, then explains the bond's controlled reversibility and limits.

questions.stem: Why does the repairer use only a small amount of paste?
choices: A small amount prevents the starch granules from absorbing any water.
A light application can make the bond while reducing the risk of staining or stiffening the page.
The paste becomes permanent whenever it touches a large sheet of paper.
A thick layer would make the adhesive dry before reaching the fibers.
questions.explanation: The text says too much paste can stain or stiffen a sheet, while a skilled application provides a light, strong connection.

questions.stem: What does “reversibility” mean in this context?
choices: The paste can be stored forever without spoiling.
The tear will close itself before paste is applied.
A trained person may later soften and change the repair with controlled moisture.
The strip of paper becomes stronger each time it is folded.
questions.explanation: The sentence before the term describes softening the water-based adhesive under controlled conditions so a later repair can be changed.

questions.stem: What leaves the mixture as the paste dries?
choices: The starch granules
The overlapping fibers
The repair strip
Water
questions.explanation: The third paragraph begins by stating that water leaves the mixture as it dries, while starch remains between fibers.

lesson.strategy: Follow where water goes. It enters swelling starch, carries paste among paper fibers, and then leaves during drying. The remaining starch creates the bond and can later respond to moisture.

skillTips.main-idea: Retell the material sequence from warming to drying, then include why controlled moisture matters after the bond forms.
skillTips.inference: Connect the warning about excess paste to the earlier small application; less paste limits stains and stiffness.
skillTips.vocabulary: The previous sentence directly demonstrates reversibility, so translate that action into a definition.
skillTips.detail: During drying, water leaves and starch remains; keep those opposite movements clear.

passages.title: Jane Addams and the Listening House
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Jane Addams was born in Illinois in 1860 and grew up wondering how a useful life might serve other people. During a visit to London, she saw Toynbee Hall, a settlement house where residents lived in a city neighborhood and organized educational and social work.

In 1889, Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull-House on Chicago's Near West Side. They first imagined a place for art and literary learning. Rather than holding tightly to that first plan, they listened as neighbors used the house and described local needs. Hull-House grew to include classes, childcare, a library, clubs, arts programs, and meeting spaces. Other residents joined the work and brought knowledge in fields such as health, labor, education, and research.

Addams treated the shared house as a place to learn with a neighborhood, not simply to deliver a fixed service. As Hull-House evolved, experience there informed her writing and her efforts for civic reform and peace. In 1931, she shared the Nobel Peace Prize. Her public honors were large, but her daily method began at a smaller scale: keep a door open, observe what happens, and let relationships reshape the work.

questions.explanation: The passage connects Addams's responsive work at Hull-House to her broader writing and reform, emphasizing listening and adaptation as her method.

They wanted every resident to work in exactly the same field.

They believed art and literary learning had no place in a shared house.
questions.explanation: They began with a narrower educational idea, listened to neighbors, and supported many additional programs as the house evolved.

lesson.strategy: Track the widening circle of Addams's work: an idea seen in London, a house opened with Starr, programs reshaped by neighbors, and experience carried into writing and reform.

passages.title: The Second-Price Auction
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In a simple sealed-bid auction, each bidder writes one offer without seeing the others. The highest bidder wins. In an ordinary first-price auction, that winner pays the amount of the winning bid. This creates a puzzle: bidding a true private value may mean paying more than necessary, so bidders often try to guess how far they can shade their offers.

A second-price auction changes the payment rule. The highest bidder still wins, but pays the second-highest bid. Suppose Nia values an item at eighty tokens. If the leading rival bids sixty, any winning bid by Nia leads to the same sixty-token price. Bidding above eighty could make her win when the price exceeds her value. Bidding below eighty could make her lose a purchase she would have valued. In this simple setting, bidding her value avoids both mistakes.

The result depends on conditions. Bidders need independent private values, clear rules, and no coordination among them. Shared estimates of resale value, budget limits, collusion, or unusual tie rules can change the strategy. An auction design does not remove every problem of information or power.

The important idea is that rules shape the thinking a market requires. By separating the winning offer from the price paid, a second-price auction can make honest revelation a practical strategy under the right assumptions.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: Every sealed-bid auction makes the winner pay exactly the amount written in the winning offer.
A second-price auction eliminates budgets, collusion, and uncertainty from every market.
Under simple private-value conditions, paying the second-highest bid can make bidding one’s true value a sensible strategy.
Bidders should always offer more than an item is worth so they cannot lose it.
questions.explanation: The passage connects the second-price payment rule with truthful bidding, while limiting that result to stated assumptions.

questions.stem: Why should Nia avoid bidding more than eighty tokens?
choices: The auction would automatically turn into a first-price auction.
Her bid would become visible before anyone else submitted an offer.
The second-highest bid would always fall to zero.
She could win when the required price is greater than the value she places on the item.
questions.explanation: An offer above her value can commit Nia to a winning outcome that costs more than the item is worth to her.

questions.stem: What does “private value” mean in this passage?
choices: The value a bidder personally places on the item rather than a value secretly fixed by the auctioneer
A price that every bidder must pay before submitting an offer
The second-highest offer after all bidders coordinate
A resale price guaranteed to be identical for everyone
questions.explanation: Nia’s eighty-token value describes what the item is worth to her, which may differ from another bidder’s value.

questions.stem: What does the winner pay in the auction described?
choices: The lowest submitted bid
The second-highest submitted bid
Twice the winning bid
The winner’s private value in every case
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid.

lesson.strategy: Separate three quantities: a bidder’s own value, the bid submitted, and the price paid. Then test why bidding above or below value can create a different mistake.

signals.means: This introduces the feature that distinguishes the auction from a first-price sale.
This closes the comparison between bidding too high and bidding too low.
This limits the strategy claim to a specific model rather than every real auction.

vocab.inContext: an auction in which offers are submitted without seeing rivals’ offers first
the worth that an individual bidder personally assigns to the item
secret coordination among bidders that undermines genuine competition

skillTips.main-idea: Include the payment rule, truthful-bidding incentive, and the assumptions that limit the result.
skillTips.inference: Compare a bid with Nia’s value and ask which losing or winning mistake becomes possible.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use Nia’s personal eighty-token judgment to distinguish private value from a shared market price.
skillTips.detail: Keep the winner-selection rule separate from the payment rule: highest wins, second-highest sets the price.

passages.title: What a Coat Hook Understands
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A coat hook is among the least impressive objects in a public room. It has no screen, offers no instructions, and disappears against the wall. Yet watch an entrance on a rainy evening. A well-placed hook receives the wet coat before it reaches a chair, frees a hand holding papers, and keeps a bag within reach. The object solves several small problems without asking anyone to announce them.

In practice, however, one hook at one height embodies a narrow guess about bodies and belongings. A row with varied heights and enough space between hooks serves more people and more kinds of objects. Placement reduces friction only when it reflects how the room is actually used. A hook hidden behind an open door may satisfy a drawing while failing every visitor.

This is why small fixtures deserve observation after installation. Scuffed paint may reveal where bags strike the wall. Coats sliding together may show that the spacing is wrong. An unused hook may indicate poor placement rather than absent need. Such evidence turns design from a proud statement into a provisional answer that can be revised.

The larger point is not that every room needs more hardware. It is that care can take physical form. Accommodation sometimes looks like a policy or a helpful person; sometimes it is a sturdy object waiting in the right place. Good shared spaces reduce the number of minor requests people must make, while remaining alert to needs their first design did not foresee.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the essay's main idea?
choices: Public rooms should replace helpful people and policies with rows of identical hooks.
A design drawing provides better evidence than watching how visitors use a finished room.
An unused fixture proves that nobody needs the service it was meant to provide.
Thoughtful small fixtures can embody care when their placement is observed, tested, and revised around real use.
questions.explanation: The essay moves from the hook's quiet help to varied placement and post-installation evidence, arguing that physical care depends on responsive design.

questions.stem: Why does the writer value scuffed paint and unused hooks as evidence?
choices: They can reveal a mismatch between the original design and people's actual movements or needs.
They prove that visitors are using every fixture exactly as planned.
They show that sturdy hardware should never be moved after installation.
They allow designers to avoid observing the room in use.
questions.explanation: The marks and patterns point to collisions, spacing, or poor placement, giving designers information for revising a provisional answer.

questions.stem: What does “provisional” mean in the third paragraph?
choices: Proudly displayed as the only possible solution
Open to revision when later evidence appears
Hidden from visitors behind an open door
Designed to hold only coats and no other objects
questions.explanation: The passage calls design a provisional answer “that can be revised,” so the word means temporary or open to change with evidence.

questions.stem: Which example does the passage give of poor hook placement?
choices: A row containing hooks at varied heights
Enough open space between neighboring hooks
A hook hidden behind an open door
A hook that keeps a bag within reach
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that a hook hidden behind an open door may satisfy a drawing while failing visitors.

lesson.strategy: Follow the essay's design loop: notice a small need, place a fixture, observe traces of real use, and revise. The coat hook matters because it makes that larger loop concrete.

signals.means: Challenges the simple one-hook solution with varied real users and objects.
Connects placement problems to the need for observation after installation.
Expands the hook example into a claim about care taking physical form.

vocab.inContext: small difficulty created when placement does not fit actual use
treated as open to revision when evidence appears
a change or support that helps meet different needs

skillTips.main-idea: Treat the hook as evidence for a larger claim about responsive care, not as an argument that every wall needs hardware.
skillTips.inference: Read scuffs and disuse as feedback rather than failure; each trace helps explain what the first placement missed.
skillTips.vocabulary: The words “can be revised” immediately unpack “provisional” and show the design is not final.
skillTips.detail: Distinguish the good placements from the bad one: varied heights and open spacing help, while the door conceals.

passages.title: The Egret and the Ripples
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At dawn, an egret stood beside a pond. The water was clear, and she could see small fish below. A young raccoon splashed into the shallows. Rings spread across the surface. The fish vanished beneath a fallen branch.

The raccoon blamed the pond for hiding his breakfast. He slapped the water again, making wider rings. The egret waited without moving. She watched the branch. When the pond grew still, one fish left the branch. The egret lowered her beak and caught it. The raccoon finally sat quietly on the bank. Soon he could see three fish that he had missed before.

Muddy water can settle on its own. A noisy search may hide the answer it seeks.

questions.stem: What lesson does this fable mainly teach?
choices: Patience lets the pond reveal what frantic splashing keeps hidden.
Clear ponds always hold more fish than muddy ponds.
Raccoons should hunt only after sunrise.
Egrets succeed because they are larger than other pond animals.
questions.explanation: The raccoon keeps disturbing the pond and cannot see fish, while the still egret waits for the water to clear and succeeds. The closing moral contrasts a noisy search with patient settling.

questions.stem: Why does the egret wait without moving?
choices: She is too tired to enter the pond.
She expects still water to make the hidden fish easier to see.
She wants the raccoon to catch every fish first.
She is afraid of the fallen branch.
questions.explanation: After the egret waits, the pond grows still and a fish leaves the branch. Her success after the ripples fade shows that stillness is her method, not fear or tiredness.

questions.stem: What does "shallows" mean in this passage?
choices: Tall plants beside the water
Dark holes beneath the pond
Water near the edge that is not deep
Wide rings made by splashing
questions.explanation: The raccoon splashes into the shallows from beside the pond. That setting supports the meaning of shallow water near the bank, not a plant, hole, or ripple.

questions.stem: Where do the fish hide after the raccoon splashes?
choices: Under the muddy bank
Behind the egret's legs
Among tall pond grass
Beneath a fallen branch
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly says that the fish vanished beneath a fallen branch after rings spread across the surface.

lesson.strategy: Track cause and result at the pond: splashing makes ripples and hides the fish, while waiting lets the water settle. Use that contrast to connect the animals' actions to the closing moral.

signals.means: Shows the immediate result of the raccoon's splash and begins his problem.
Marks the patient action that contrasts with the raccoon's noisy search.
Signals the condition that lets the hidden fish appear again.

vocab.inContext: water near the bank that is not deep
went out of sight very quickly
become calm and clear after being stirred

skillTips.main-idea: Match the final two sentences to both animals: the raccoon hides his answer, while the egret lets it appear.
skillTips.inference: Notice what happens immediately after the egret waits. The calm water explains the purpose of her stillness.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the pond bank and the raccoon's splash to picture shallows as water that is close to land and not deep.
skillTips.detail: Follow the fish from visible water to their hiding place beneath the branch, then back into view after the pond calms.

passages.title: What Walkers Owe a Trail
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A trail is often treated as an invitation: the ground is open, so anyone may pass. Yet every step changes the path a little. Boots press soil, shortcuts widen bare patches, and careless hands move stones that guide water. No single visitor creates the whole problem, but each visitor adds to it.

This shared effect raises a simple question: what does a walker owe to people who come later? The answer cannot be to leave no trace at all, because walking itself makes a trace. A better duty is restraint: use the durable path, leave plants and markers in place, and carry away what you brought. Restraint accepts that enjoyment and care belong together. A place can welcome us without becoming ours to rearrange.

This duty also runs in both directions. Past walkers and trail crews made today's journey possible. By protecting the route, a present visitor returns part of that gift to strangers not yet seen.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the passage's main idea?
choices: Walking should be banned wherever footsteps can press the soil.
Shared enjoyment of a trail creates a duty to limit damage for later visitors.
Trail crews alone are responsible for keeping every route usable.
A visitor owns any natural place that welcomes public use.
questions.explanation: The passage accepts that walking leaves some trace, then defines restraint as using the durable path and preserving plants and markers. Its duty reaches both past helpers and future visitors.

questions.stem: Why does the author say that the duty runs in both directions?
choices: Every trail must allow travel in two physical directions.
Visitors should divide their walks equally between old and new routes.
Today's walkers receive care from earlier people and can pass that care to future strangers.
Trail crews and visitors should exchange their jobs each season.
questions.explanation: Past walkers and crews made the present journey possible, while present care protects the route for people who come later. The two directions are backward and forward in time.

questions.stem: What does "restraint" mean as it is used here?
choices: A rope placed beside a dangerous trail
A demand that nobody enjoy the outdoors
A plan to make every path completely unchanged
A deliberate limit on one's actions to avoid needless harm
questions.explanation: The examples after restraint all limit what a walker does: stay on the durable path, leave objects in place, and remove belongings. The word means chosen self-control.

questions.stem: Which actions does the passage give as examples of restraint?
choices: Use the durable path, leave plants and markers, and carry out what you brought.
Build shortcuts, move stones, and mark every place you visit.
Avoid all trails that have been used by earlier walkers.
Repair bridges and replace every sign before leaving.
questions.explanation: The middle paragraph lists those three actions immediately after naming restraint. The other choices add damage, demand no use, or assign visitors work the text does not require.

lesson.strategy: Read this as a claim built from a tension: walking changes a trail, yet people may still enjoy it. The proposed answer is restraint, shown through three concrete visitor choices.

signals.phrase: Yet every step changes the path a little.
signals.means: Introduces the tension between an open invitation and the effects of use.

signals.phrase: This shared effect raises a simple question
signals.means: Turns several small physical changes into an ethical question about duty.
States the passage's practical answer after rejecting an impossible standard.

vocab.inContext: chosen limits that prevent needless damage
able to withstand repeated use without easy damage
move or change things into a different order

skillTips.main-idea: Keep both sides of the argument: trails invite use, but shared use creates a duty of care toward other people.
skillTips.inference: Translate both directions into time. Earlier care reaches the present walker, whose care can reach future walkers.
skillTips.vocabulary: Let the examples define restraint. Each one is a choice to limit interference rather than a ban on walking.
skillTips.detail: Find the sentence after the colon following restraint; it supplies the exact three actions the question asks for.

passages.title: The Pause Before a Conclusion
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
During field observations, people often write the name of an object as soon as they recognize it: oak leaf, sparrow, storm cloud. A label is useful, but it can also end the search. Once the observer writes sparrow, the mind may stop checking the beak, tail, movement, or call. The quick answer feels complete even when important features remain unseen.

One way to resist this early finish is to separate description from interpretation. In one column, record only visible or audible details: three dark wing bars, a repeated high note, feeding near the ground. In another, write the possible identification and any doubt. This small pause turns observation into a test rather than a guess.

The method does not forbid intuition. An experienced observer often notices patterns quickly. Instead, the two columns preserve the evidence that supports or challenges that first impression. They also make later correction easier, because another person can examine the notes. Careful seeing begins when naming becomes a question, not the end of one.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: Experienced field observers should trust their first labels without recording details.
Naming an object is less useful than making an artistic drawing of it.
Separating raw observations from interpretations keeps an early label open to testing and correction.
Two-column notebooks are valuable mainly because they hold twice as many field notes.
questions.explanation: The passage warns that an early label may stop further checking. Its two-column method preserves observed features separately so the proposed identification can be tested and corrected.

questions.stem: Why can another person examine the two-column notes more effectively?
choices: The observer has removed every uncertain detail from the record.
The possible identification is guaranteed to be correct.
The second person already knows what species was present.
The visible evidence remains available apart from the first observer's conclusion.
questions.explanation: One column records features while the other holds the possible identification. Because the evidence is preserved separately, another reader can compare it with or against the conclusion.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, what does "preserve" mean?
choices: Keep something available so it can be examined later
Hide something so nobody can challenge it
Replace a weak idea with a certain answer
Shorten a record by removing small details
questions.explanation: The evidence in the two columns supports later correction and examination by another person. Preserve therefore means keeping that evidence available, not hiding or reducing it.

questions.stem: What belongs in the first column of the suggested field notes?
choices: Only the final name of the object
Visible or audible details without an identification
A list of what other observers believe
Questions that cannot be answered outdoors
questions.explanation: The passage directs the observer to record only visible or audible details in the first column, then place the possible identification and doubt in the second.

lesson.strategy: Follow the passage's problem-method-benefit structure. First labeling can stop attention; separate columns slow that finish; preserved evidence then supports review and correction.

signals.means: Marks the moment when a useful label may prematurely stop closer checking.
