Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. A childhood injury left him unable to see, but he kept learning through touch and sound. At a school for blind students in Paris, he read books made with raised print. The letters could be felt, yet they were large and slow to read.

As a teenager, Braille learned about a code of raised dots designed for messages in darkness. He reshaped the idea into cells of six dots. Different patterns could represent letters, numbers, and music. Readers could recognize a whole cell under one fingertip, and they could write with simple tools.

Braille later taught at the same school. His system was not accepted everywhere during his life, but students valued its speed and clarity. Over time, the six-dot method spread widely. Braille's work gave blind readers a practical way to read, write, study, and share ideas for themselves.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of this biography?
choices: Louis Braille became known mainly for teaching music at a school in Paris.
Louis Braille transformed a raised-dot code into a practical reading and writing system.
Raised print became faster to read after schools made each letter much larger.
Blind students stopped using simple writing tools during Braille's lifetime.
questions.explanation: The biography traces how Braille adapted raised dots into six-dot cells that readers could use efficiently for language, numbers, and music.

questions.stem: Why did students likely value Braille's system even before it was widely accepted?
choices: It removed the need to learn letters or numbers.
It turned every schoolbook into a book about music.
It was faster and gave them a practical way to read and write.
It allowed them to read ordinary ink without using touch.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts slow raised print with the speed and clarity of six-dot cells that readers could recognize and write themselves.

questions.stem: What does “raised” mean in the phrase “raised print”?
choices: Moved to a higher shelf
Made louder for a group
Taught by an older student
Lifted above the flat surface
questions.explanation: The letters were designed to be felt by touch, so “raised” means they stood above the flat page.

questions.stem: How many dots formed the cells in Braille's system?
choices: Six dots
Four dots
Eight dots
Ten dots
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that Braille reshaped the earlier idea into cells of six dots.

lesson.strategy: Follow the problem-and-improvement chain: raised print was slow, Braille adapted a dot code, and six-dot cells gave readers a faster practical system.

signals.means: Shows that Braille continued his education despite losing his sight.
Locates the stage of life when Braille encountered and reshaped the dot code.
Shows that broad acceptance and use developed gradually rather than immediately.

vocab.inContext: Standing above a flat page so the shape can be felt by touch.
Small groups of six dot positions used to form symbols.
The quality of being easy to recognize and understand.

skillTips.main-idea: Select the choice that names both Braille's adaptation and the practical reading and writing result.
skillTips.inference: Compare the slow raised letters with the six-dot cells' stated speed, clarity, and ease of writing.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the phrase “could be felt” to understand how raised print differs from flat ink.
skillTips.detail: Look for the number attached directly to the word “cells” in the second paragraph.

passages.title: The Deposit That Brings a Bottle Back
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A drink container may be worth little after it is empty. Dropping it in a bin is easy, while carrying it to a collection point takes effort. A refundable deposit changes that choice. The buyer pays a small extra amount and receives it back when the container is returned.

The deposit gives the empty container a visible value. A person who would have discarded it now has a reason to return it. Someone else may collect an abandoned container and claim the refund, so the incentive can work even after the first buyer walks away. Returned containers can then enter a reuse or recycling system with less litter and more predictable material.

The system is not costless. Shops or machines need space, staff, transport, and rules for damaged containers. A deposit set too low may not change behavior; one set high creates a larger payment before the refund. Some deposits are never claimed. Those funds do not erase the inconvenience faced by people far from a return point.

A deposit therefore joins a price signal to a collection system. The money matters because return is possible, and the return network matters because the money can be recovered.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A container deposit makes every shop accept every damaged object without cost.
Unclaimed deposits remove the need for convenient collection points.
A refundable deposit can encourage container returns, but its success also depends on a usable collection system.
The best deposit is always the largest amount a buyer can pay.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the return incentive and balances it against collection costs, deposit size, and access.

questions.stem: Why might someone collect a container another person abandoned?
choices: The container becomes impossible to recycle after purchase.
The original buyer must approve every later return.
A shop pays extra for litter left nearby.
The collector may return it and receive the refundable deposit.
questions.explanation: The refund remains attached to returning the container, so another person can respond to the same incentive.

questions.stem: What does “refundable” mean here?
choices: Able to be paid back when a stated condition is met
Too small to influence any decision
Collected only when a container is damaged
Permanently added to the drink’s price
questions.explanation: The extra amount is paid back after the buyer or collector returns the container.

questions.stem: Which problem can make returning a container harder?
choices: A visible refund value
Living far from a return point
A predictable supply of material
Another person collecting litter
questions.explanation: The third paragraph notes the inconvenience faced by people who are far from a return point.

lesson.strategy: Trace the loop from extra payment to empty container, return, and refund. Then identify the infrastructure and tradeoffs required to complete that loop.

signals.means: This introduces the incentive that makes returning more attractive than discarding.
This turns from the return benefit to operating and access burdens.
This combines the price signal and collection network into one conclusion.

vocab.inContext: paid back after the container is returned as required
a reason that can make returning the container more attractive
requested and received by completing the return

skillTips.main-idea: State both parts of the system: money encourages return, and accessible collection makes the refund usable.
skillTips.inference: Follow the refund rather than ownership; the person who returns the container can respond to its value.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the opening payment-and-return sequence to define refundable as able to be paid back.
skillTips.detail: Find the access problem among the operating limits in the third paragraph.

passages.title: The Honest Estimate
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At a repair counter, certainty can sound like competence. A customer brings in a silent mixer or a lamp that flickers, and the worker wants to offer one cause, one price, and one date. That clean answer is comforting. It may also be fiction.

An honest estimate is not a shrug. It separates what can be seen from what must be discovered. The cracked cord has a known cost; the hidden damage inside the motor does not. A careful worker can explain the first test, give a reasonable range, and name the point when new permission will be needed. This turns uncertainty into a plan instead of a surprise.

The same habit belongs outside repair shops. Editors cannot know how many revisions an argument will need, and builders sometimes uncover trouble behind a wall. Pretending otherwise moves risk onto the person who has less information. By contrast, a clear estimate shares both knowledge and doubt.

We often treat trust as a reward for being right. I think it grows more reliably when people show where their knowledge ends and promise the next clear step. Accuracy matters, but so does honest revision. A useful estimate is therefore not a prediction carved in stone. It is an agreement about how two people will proceed as reality becomes clearer.

questions.stem: What central idea does the essay develop?
choices: Customers should avoid asking about cost until every repair has been completed.
A skilled worker can always identify one cause and one exact price at first inspection.
Estimates are useful only in repair shops because other work contains little uncertainty.
An honest estimate builds trust by naming uncertainty and setting a clear next step.
questions.explanation: The essay argues that trustworthy estimates distinguish known facts from uncertainty and create an agreement about what happens next.

questions.stem: Why can false certainty place risk on the person with less information?
choices: That person may make plans based on a price or date that was never well supported.
That person automatically gains the right to approve every future test.
The worker must then reveal every technique used in the repair.
The known cost of a visible part will always become higher.
questions.explanation: The essay contrasts invented certainty with a range and checkpoints, implying that unsupported promises can leave the customer carrying the surprise.

questions.stem: What does “competence” most nearly mean in the first sentence?
choices: A desire to finish before others
The ability to do work skillfully
A written promise about a price
The cost of discovering hidden damage
questions.explanation: Certainty can make a worker sound capable and professional, so “competence” refers to the ability to perform work skillfully.

questions.stem: Which contrast does the essay use to show known and unknown costs?
choices: A new lamp and an old mixer
An editor's draft and a builder's wall
A cracked cord and hidden motor damage
A finished repair and a signed invoice
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says a cracked cord has a known cost while hidden damage inside the motor does not.

lesson.strategy: Track the essay's distinction between known facts and hidden conditions, then notice how ranges, permission points, and revision turn uncertainty into cooperation.

signals.means: Challenges the comforting assumption that a clean, certain answer must be true.
Opposes unsupported certainty with an estimate that shares knowledge and doubt.

signals.phrase: therefore not a prediction carved in stone
signals.means: Draws the conclusion that an estimate should guide cooperation, not claim certainty.

vocab.inContext: The ability to perform a task with knowledge and skill.
A reasoned judgment of likely cost, time, or work before all facts are known.
A change made when new evidence shows that an earlier view needs updating.

passages.title: The Scale and the Scoop
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the town granary, a brass Scale and a wooden Scoop worked beside the same bins. The Scale took pride in making every measure exact. The Scoop valued speed and could fill a sack before the Scale had settled its needle. Each considered the other's talent a flaw: the Scale called haste careless, while the Scoop called precision useless delay.

After heavy rain washed out a road, the steward had one afternoon to divide seed grain among farmers before the remaining bridge closed for repairs. The Scale began alone. Every sack was equal, but the line barely moved. The Scoop pushed forward and filled six sacks quickly, but one bulged while another remained light. Farmers at the back watched the sky and worried they would leave with nothing.

A young storekeeper placed the Scoop at the bin and the Scale at the tying table. The Scoop filled each sack almost to its mark. The Scale then added or removed a small amount before the cord was pulled tight. Their former weaknesses disappeared inside the new sequence. By dusk, the final cart crossed the bridge with a fair share.

The Scale still guarded fairness, and the Scoop still guarded time. Neither had surrendered its nature. They had learned that a tool becomes wiser when its limits shape the work around it. From then on, the granary judged a method not by the perfection of one step, but by whether the whole task served everyone.

choices: A strong system can combine different strengths so the whole task is both fair and timely.

Tools should work alone because a sequence hides each tool's natural talent.
Fair shares are possible only when every sack is filled by the same tool.
questions.explanation: Neither tool succeeds alone, but the storekeeper's sequence combines the Scoop's speed with the Scale's precision and serves everyone.

questions.stem: Why does the storekeeper place the Scoop before the Scale in the new sequence?

Quick filling handles most of the work, and precise checking corrects the final amount.

Precise checking makes the bridge remain open longer.

Gave up or abandoned

lesson.strategy: Compare each tool working alone with the two-step sequence. The fable's lesson comes from how the storekeeper designs around speed, precision, and their limits.

passages.title: The Rule You Would Share
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A rule feels easy when it helps us. The harder test comes when the same rule helps someone else. Suppose you step ahead in a line whenever your own errand feels urgent. If everyone did that, soon no one could trust the order.

This test asks us to share the rule, not just the benefit. Before choosing, imagine every person making the same choice. Would the system still work? Would the rule seem fair when another person used it against your plans? A good rule does not need to favor everyone in every moment. Still, it should make cooperation possible for all. It asks whether our reason can be offered to others without a special exception for ourselves. Thinking this way turns a private excuse into a public question.

questions.explanation: The example says that if everyone stepped ahead, soon no one could trust the order that makes a line useful.

Making a choice in private

Working together for a shared result
questions.explanation: The rule must let a shared system work for all, so “cooperation” means people working together successfully.

passages.title: Learning by Explaining
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Reading a set of instructions can make an idea feel familiar. Explaining the idea to another person is a stronger test. The speaker must choose an order, connect each step, and replace vague words with clear ones. A missing link that stayed hidden during silent reading may suddenly become obvious.

Questions make the test even better. A listener may ask why a step matters or what would happen in a different case. If the speaker cannot answer, the pause marks a useful gap in understanding. The goal is not to perform perfectly. It is to find what needs more thought.

This is why teaching can strengthen the teacher's learning. After an explanation, the speaker can return to the source, correct an error, and try again. Familiarity only signals that the material has been seen before. A clear explanation demands more: the ability to rebuild an idea so another person can use it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Silent reading is the only dependable way to notice a missing step in an idea.
A good teacher should answer every question correctly on the first attempt.
Explaining an idea can deepen learning by exposing gaps and forcing clear connections.
Familiar material no longer needs to be checked against its original source.
questions.explanation: The passage shows that explaining requires structure and clarity, while questions expose gaps that the speaker can revisit and correct.

questions.stem: Why are a listener's questions useful to the person explaining?
choices: They allow the speaker to avoid organizing the steps.
They prove that the source contains no errors.

questions.explanation: When the speaker cannot answer, the pause identifies a gap, giving the speaker a specific place to review and improve.

choices: Not clear or specific
Arranged in a useful order
Easy to prove with one example
Repeated exactly from memory
questions.explanation: The speaker replaces vague words with clear ones, so “vague” means unclear or lacking specific meaning.

choices: Stop using the original material
Return to the source, correct an error, and try again
Replace every clear word with a familiar one

questions.explanation: The final paragraph directly lists returning to the source, correcting an error, and trying the explanation again.

lesson.strategy: Follow the passage's learning loop: organize an explanation, notice the gap revealed by a question, return to the source, and explain again more clearly.

signals.means: Shows that listener questions strengthen the test created by explaining.

Connects the earlier evidence about gaps to the conclusion about teaching and learning.

skillTips.inference: Treat an unanswered question as evidence about the speaker's understanding, not as a failure by the listener.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the direct contrast between “vague words” and “clear ones” to determine the meaning.
skillTips.detail: Scan the final paragraph for the three actions the speaker can take after an explanation.

passages.title: Why a Ratchet Clicks
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A socket wrench can tighten a bolt without making a full circle. Inside its head is a ratchet, a wheel with angled teeth. A small catch called a pawl rests against those teeth. When the handle moves in the working direction, the pawl pushes the wheel and turns the socket.

On the return stroke, the angled surfaces lift the pawl over each tooth. The wheel stays almost still while the handle moves back, producing the familiar clicks. Because the tool does not undo its last turn, a worker can reset the handle in a narrow space. A switch changes which side of the teeth the pawl engages, so the same wrench can tighten or loosen.

The design converts back-and-forth motion into one-way steps. Similar mechanisms appear in winches and other devices that must hold progress between strokes. The teeth and pawl carry repeated forces, so dirt or wear can make them slip. Cleaning, correct lubrication, and replacing damaged parts help preserve the grip. The useful feature is not the clicking sound itself; it is the controlled direction hidden beneath the sound.

choices: A ratchet's clicking sound warns that its teeth must be replaced immediately.
A socket wrench tightens only when its handle can move through a complete circle.
A pawl is used mainly to add oil to the moving parts inside a wrench.
A ratchet uses teeth and a pawl to turn in controlled steps while the handle resets.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how the pawl drives the toothed wheel one way, slides over it on return, and lets the handle reset.

questions.stem: Why is a ratchet especially useful in a narrow space?
choices: The handle can move back and forth without undoing the previous turn.
The pawl makes the bolt smaller after every click.
The switch removes the need for teeth inside the tool.
The wrench can operate without touching the bolt.
questions.explanation: The handle can reset on the return stroke while the wheel holds its progress, so it does not need room for a full circle.

questions.stem: What does “engages” mean in the sentence about the switch?
choices: Moves away from permanently
Makes working contact with
Measures the width of
Cleans dirt from
questions.explanation: The switch changes the side where the pawl meets and works against the teeth, so “engages” means makes working contact with.

questions.stem: What does the switch on the wrench change?
choices: The amount of dirt inside the head
The size of the socket opening
Which side of the teeth the pawl engages
How many bolts the wrench can hold
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that the switch changes which side of the angled teeth the pawl engages.

lesson.strategy: Mentally separate the wrench into a working stroke and a return stroke. Track what the pawl does in each direction to explain both the clicks and the held progress.

signals.means: Moves the explanation from the force-producing motion to the resetting motion.

signals.means: Gives the reason a ratchet works where a full handle circle is impossible.

skillTips.inference: Connect limited space with the handle's ability to return without reversing the socket's progress.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the nearby switch and direction change to infer that “engages” describes working contact.

passages.title: The Quiet Cart
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Joon's maintenance cart announced him before he reached any door. One wheel clicked, the metal trays rattled, and a loose latch chimed at every floor seam. During the day, no one minded. On the guesthouse night shift, each sound seemed to travel through the sleeping building.

The replacement cart would not arrive for a month. Joon first wrapped a towel around the trays, but it slipped and caught the drawer. He then remembered the felt circles his aunt placed beneath chair legs in her upstairs apartment. From a scrap box, he cut narrow felt washers for the tray brackets and a thicker pad for the latch. The rattle faded, yet the wheel still clicked.

At breakfast, the cook lent him a wooden skewer to use as a fixed guide. Joon lifted the cart, held the skewer beside the rim, and spun the wheel. The changing gap showed that the wheel sat crooked. A careful adjustment centered its axle. That evening, the cart crossed the lobby with only a soft roll.

The manager praised Joon for fixing the cart before its replacement arrived. Joon pointed toward the kitchen and shared the credit. His aunt's chair pads had inspired the felt, and the cook's guide had exposed the crooked wheel. The cart rolled softly because he had carried two familiar ideas into a new problem.

choices: He wants the manager to move the cart away from the guest rooms.

questions.explanation: The cook supplied the fixed guide that exposed the crooked wheel, so Joon shares credit for a repair built from several people's ideas.

choices: A mark showing where a wheel touched

questions.explanation: The latch is a loose cart part that receives a felt pad; in context, it is the fastener that holds a drawer or section closed.

choices: A cover for the entire cart

questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that Joon cuts narrow felt washers for the tray brackets and a thicker pad for the latch.

passages.title: The Workshop's Bridge and Gate
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In many medieval European towns, skilled trades were organized through guilds. These associations set rules for crafts such as weaving, metalworking, and leatherwork. They also shaped how knowledge moved from an experienced maker to a beginner. Because techniques were carried in hands as well as words, learning usually happened beside the work.

An apprentice entered a master's household or shop for a period of training. The beginner handled simple duties first, observed repeated processes, and gradually practiced more demanding tasks. Agreements varied by place and trade, but the master generally owed instruction and supervision, while the apprentice owed labor and obedience. This arrangement could teach details that a short written recipe could not capture: the sound of a well-struck tool or the feel of properly worked material.

After training, a worker might become a journeyman and earn wages. Journeymen could deepen their skill in other shops before seeking the status of master. A guild might require evidence of competence, sometimes through an especially demanding piece of work. The familiar word masterpiece grew from this world of judged craft.

The system preserved knowledge and gave buyers some assurance about workmanship. However, guild control could also restrict who entered a trade, limit competition, and defend old methods. Apprenticeship was therefore both an educational bridge and a guarded gate. Its history shows that passing on skill is never only a private act; rules about teaching also decide who gets the chance to learn.

questions.explanation: The passage explains both apprenticeship's educational role and the guild's power to guard entry, summarized as a bridge and a gate.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the sound of a struck tool and the feel of worked material as details that a short recipe could not fully convey.

passages.title: How Mussels Hold On
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A mussel lives where moving water can pull hard. It cannot hold a rock with hands or claws. Instead, its foot places thin, sticky threads against the surface. These strong lines are called byssal threads. The mussel makes them from proteins and attaches them to the rock one by one.

One thread is small, but many threads share the force of a wave. Rough water pulls in different directions, so a bundle is safer than a single stiff link. The threads bend without letting the mussel drift away. If a thread breaks, the animal can make a new one. The mussel may also release old threads when it needs to move a short distance. This natural anchor is both firm and flexible. It shows how many light connections can do the work of one heavy chain.

passages.title: When One Shift Hands Work Over
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When one work shift ends, unfinished tasks do not disappear. A clear handoff tells the next worker what has happened, what still needs attention, and what may be unusual. It can be spoken, written, or both. The form matters less than the shared picture it creates.

A useful handoff names specific facts. It may record that a delivery is late, a valve is closed for repair, or a customer is waiting for a reply. It also separates completed work from planned work. Otherwise, the next person may repeat a task or assume it was done.

Good handoffs are brief enough to use and detailed enough to guide action. A standard list can protect easily forgotten items, while a short conversation allows questions. The goal is continuity, not a perfect report. When workers leave one another a reliable starting point, the job becomes less dependent on any single person's memory.

passages.title: Why Metal Breaks at the Bend
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Bend a metal paper clip once, and it usually keeps its new shape. Bend the same spot back and forth many times, and the clip eventually breaks. The force is not spread across the whole object. It is concentrated in a narrow region where the metal repeatedly changes direction.

Metal is made of crystals whose atoms sit in ordered patterns. Under force, tiny defects in those patterns allow layers to shift. Repeated bending rearranges and blocks that movement, making the worked area harder to deform. At the same time, microscopic cracks can begin near the surface, especially where scratches or sharp corners concentrate stress.

Each new bend opens those cracks a little farther. The unbroken section then carries more of the load, so the damage speeds up until the remaining metal separates. Engineers call this kind of failure fatigue. A part can therefore break under repeated forces that would not snap it in one attempt. Rounded corners, smoother surfaces, and loads kept within a suitable range can slow the process. The broken clip offers a small example of why machines must be designed for repetition, not merely for one strong push.

choices: Repeated bending concentrates damage and grows tiny cracks until metal finally breaks.

Rounded corners make metal parts fail faster by focusing stress in one place.
questions.explanation: The passage traces repeated force from a narrow bend through blocked movement and growing microscopic cracks to fatigue failure.

questions.stem: Why can a scratch make repeated-force failure more likely?
choices: It spreads every load evenly across the entire part.
It can concentrate stress where a microscopic crack begins.
It changes metal crystals into a softer material.
It prevents the unbroken section from carrying any load.
questions.explanation: The passage says cracks can begin where scratches concentrate stress, giving repeated bending a place to extend the damage.

questions.stem: What does “concentrated” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: Removed from the object
Measured after the break
Focused in a small area
Changed into a liquid
questions.explanation: The force is described as acting in a narrow region rather than across the whole object, so it is focused there.

questions.stem: Which design choices can slow the failure process?
choices: Sharper corners and rougher surfaces
Larger scratches and stronger single pushes
More bends focused on the same point
Rounded corners, smoother surfaces, and suitable loads
questions.explanation: The final paragraph directly names rounded corners, smoother surfaces, and loads kept within a suitable range.

lesson.strategy: Follow the causal chain at one bend: repeated force changes the worked region, small cracks begin, the remaining metal carries more load, and fatigue ends in separation.

signals.means: Adds crack formation to the changes already occurring inside the repeatedly bent metal.
Connects the shrinking unbroken section with faster crack growth.
Draws the conclusion that repetition can break a part without one overwhelming force.

vocab.inContext: Focused within a narrow region instead of spread across the whole object.
So small that the cracks are not readily visible without magnification.
Failure caused by damage that grows under repeated forces.

skillTips.main-idea: Choose the answer that preserves the complete sequence from repeated bending to growing cracks and final failure.
skillTips.inference: Link scratches with concentrated stress, then connect concentrated stress to the places where cracks begin.

passages.title: Leonardo's Workshop Education
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Leonardo da Vinci is often pictured as a solitary genius, but his education began in a busy Florentine workshop. As a young man, he trained with Andrea del Verrocchio, whose shop produced paintings, sculpture, metalwork, and decorations. Assistants prepared materials, copied designs, and contributed to large commissions. Learning came through observation, repeated practice, and correction by more experienced hands.

This mixed setting mattered. Grinding pigments required attention to minerals and oils; casting metal demanded knowledge of heat and molds; drawing trained the eye to notice proportion and movement. Leonardo did not have to treat art and mechanics as separate worlds because the workshop joined them in daily work.

He later filled notebooks with studies of bodies, water, machines, buildings, and flight. Many proposed devices were never constructed, so the drawings should not be mistaken for a catalog of finished inventions. The pages are valuable not because every idea succeeded, but because they preserve a mind testing relationships across fields. Diagrams sit beside reminders, revisions, and unanswered questions.

Leonardo's achievements were remarkable, yet the workshop makes their origin less mysterious. His individual curiosity grew within a community that supplied tools, problems, standards, and criticism. The biography of a maker is therefore also a biography of learning: even unusual invention begins with borrowed methods before it becomes something new.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the biography?
choices: Leonardo's notebooks mattered because every machine in them was built and worked exactly as drawn.
Leonardo's broad creativity grew from individual curiosity shaped by practical workshop learning.
Verrocchio's workshop kept painting completely separate from metalwork and mechanical problems.
Leonardo stopped learning from other people as soon as he began to draw in notebooks.
questions.explanation: The passage connects Leonardo's curiosity and later cross-field studies to the mixed skills, correction, tools, and standards of his workshop education.

questions.stem: How did the workshop likely encourage Leonardo to connect art and mechanics?
choices: It required assistants to study only one material for life.
It rejected any design that included an unanswered question.
Its daily work brought drawing, materials, heat, molds, and movement together.
It allowed only finished machines to appear in notebooks.
questions.explanation: The workshop combined painting, sculpture, metalwork, and decoration, so practical problems from several fields met in the same learning environment.

questions.stem: What are “commissions” in the first paragraph?
choices: Private corrections made in a notebook
Tools borrowed from another workshop
Questions that an assistant cannot answer
Works requested or assigned by clients
questions.explanation: The shop produced large works to which assistants contributed, so “commissions” are projects requested or assigned by clients.

questions.stem: What subjects does the passage say Leonardo studied in his notebooks?
choices: Bodies, water, machines, buildings, and flight
Only pigments, oils, and finished paintings
Guild prices, customer lists, and shop wages
Leatherwork, weaving, farming, and navigation
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly lists bodies, water, machines, buildings, and flight among Leonardo's notebook studies.

lesson.strategy: Challenge the lone-genius image by tracking what the workshop supplied: mixed materials, skilled correction, shared problems, and methods that Leonardo later extended.

signals.means: Contrasts the image of solitary genius with Leonardo's collaborative training.
Signals why a workshop joining several arts and materials shaped his thinking.
Qualifies Leonardo's remarkable achievement by returning to its social origins.

vocab.inContext: Works requested from a shop, often with assistants contributing to completion.
The size relationship among parts of a figure or design.
Changes that reconsider or improve an earlier note, drawing, or idea.

skillTips.main-idea: Join Leonardo's individual curiosity with the workshop community; the passage deliberately refuses a one-sided explanation.
skillTips.inference: Use the range of materials and processes in one shop to explain why art and mechanics could connect.
skillTips.vocabulary: Infer “commissions” from the shop producing large works with contributions from several assistants.
skillTips.detail: Find the five notebook subjects grouped in the opening sentence of the third paragraph.

passages.title: The Cost Hidden in a Spare Part
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The purchase price of a machine is only the first entry in its economic story. A bakery mixer, farm pump, or factory motor also requires maintenance, trained labor, and occasional replacement parts. If one small component is unavailable, a valuable machine may sit idle even though most of it still works. The cheap machine can then become the costly choice.

Spare parts create their own tradeoff. Keeping every possible component on a shelf ties up money and storage space, and some pieces may never be used. Keeping too few parts reduces inventory cost but increases the chance of a long interruption. Managers therefore weigh the likelihood of failure, the delay in obtaining a part, and the cost of stopped work.

Design can change this calculation. When several machines use the same belt, bearing, or fastener, one stock of parts can support them all. Replaceable modules may shorten repair time, although a whole module can cost more than its failed piece. Clear manuals and accessible components also reduce the labor needed to diagnose and complete a repair.

These costs are often hidden at the moment of sale because they arrive later and fall on different budgets. Looking at total cost of ownership brings them into one comparison. It does not mean the most repairable machine is always best. It means a buyer should value availability, downtime, and future work alongside the number printed on the invoice.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Keeping every possible spare part is always the least expensive choice for a business.
The machine with the lowest invoice price always has the lowest total cost of ownership.
A machine's real economic cost includes maintenance, parts, labor, and downtime as well as purchase price.
Replaceable modules remove every tradeoff between repair time and the price of components.
questions.explanation: The passage expands cost beyond the sale price and examines inventory, design, labor, availability, and interruptions over the machine's use.

questions.stem: Why can standard parts used by several machines reduce economic cost?
choices: They guarantee that no machine will ever fail.
They make trained repair labor unnecessary.
They remove the need to compare purchase prices.
One smaller stock of parts can meet several machines' repair needs.
questions.explanation: The text says one stock can support several machines that share components, reducing the variety of spare parts that must be held.

questions.stem: What does “inventory” mean in this passage?
choices: The stock of parts kept available for future use
The labor required to diagnose a broken machine
The price printed on the original invoice
The time during which production has stopped
questions.explanation: The sentence discusses keeping components on a shelf and the cost of keeping too few, so “inventory” is the stock held for use.

questions.stem: Which factors do managers weigh when deciding how many spare parts to keep?
choices: The machine's color, size, and place on the floor
Failure likelihood, delivery delay, and the cost of stopped work
The age of the manual, invoice paper, and storage shelf
Customer demand, advertising cost, and employee travel
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly lists failure likelihood, the delay in getting a part, and the cost of an interruption.

lesson.strategy: Build the machine's lifetime cost in layers: purchase, stocked parts, interruption risk, repair labor, and design. Then evaluate the tradeoffs rather than seeking one universal choice.

signals.means: Marks the interruption risk that rises when a business keeps fewer parts.
Qualifies the time benefit of modular repair with a possible higher part cost.
Prevents the conclusion from becoming the absolute claim that repairability always wins.

vocab.inContext: A stock of components kept available for later repair needs.
To identify the likely cause of a machine's problem.
A period when equipment cannot operate and useful work stops.

skillTips.main-idea: Reject answers based only on the invoice; the passage repeatedly adds later costs and operating consequences.
skillTips.inference: Connect common components with the statement that one stock of parts can support several machines.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the nearby images of components kept on a shelf and parts being too few to define inventory.
skillTips.detail: Find the three factors after “weigh” in the second paragraph and preserve all three.

passages.title: Passing On a Small Skill
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At the community garden, Mara showed me how to tie a young tomato plant. She made a loose loop that held the stem without squeezing it. I copied her knot, but mine slipped. Mara slowed down and let my hands follow hers. We tested the tie by sliding one finger beneath it, leaving room for the stem to grow.

A year later, a new gardener asked me for help. I began with Mara's words, then added one detail that had helped me practice. The new gardener tied the loop twice and smiled when it held. That small moment changed how I see teaching. A skill does not pass forward by staying exactly the same. Each learner keeps what works and makes the path clearer for the next person.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Tomato plants grow best when every gardener uses a different kind of knot.
A teacher should give words but never allow a learner to practice by hand.
A small skill loses its value when a later learner adds a helpful detail.
A useful skill can pass forward as each learner practices it and improves the explanation.
questions.explanation: The writer learns a tie from Mara, adds a useful detail, and teaches it onward, showing knowledge preserved through thoughtful change.

questions.stem: Why do Mara and the writer slide one finger beneath the tie?
choices: To check that the loop leaves room and does not squeeze the growing stem
To make the loose loop slip off the plant at once
To measure how many tomatoes the plant will grow
To cut the knot without touching the stem
questions.explanation: The text says the loose loop holds without squeezing and that the finger test leaves room for the stem to grow.

questions.stem: What does “loose” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: Pulled as tight as possible
Not tight, with some room to move
Broken into several pieces
Hidden beneath the soil
questions.explanation: The loop holds the stem without squeezing it and leaves growing room, so “loose” means not tight.

questions.stem: What does Mara do after the writer's first knot slips?
choices: She asks a new gardener to finish it.
She ties the plant tightly with two loops.
She slows down and lets the writer's hands follow hers.
She removes the tomato plant from the garden.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly states that Mara slows down and lets the writer's hands follow hers after the knot slips.

lesson.strategy: Follow the skill across three people: Mara shows the writer, the writer practices, and a new gardener receives the lesson with one useful addition.

signals.means: Introduces the mistake that leads Mara to demonstrate more slowly.
Moves forward to the moment when the learner becomes the teacher.
Shows how the writer preserves Mara's lesson while making it clearer.

vocab.inContext: Not tight, so the growing stem still has room.
Repeated effort that helps a person learn a skill.
An ability learned through teaching and practice.

skillTips.main-idea: Track what stays the same and what improves as the tie passes from one learner to the next.
skillTips.inference: Connect the loose loop and growing stem to the reason for checking the space with one finger.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use “without squeezing” and “room for the stem” as direct clues for “loose.”
skillTips.detail: Return to the sentence after the slipping knot to identify Mara's exact response.

passages.title: The Finch and the Rain Cups
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A finch planned to build her nest in the lowest fork of an orchard tree. A snail warned that spring water sometimes crossed that fork, but the bright ground looked dry. Instead of arguing, the snail placed three leaf cups beneath nearby branches. After each shower, he marked the water in every cup with berry dye.

The finch watched one cup fill quickly and decided the snail had proved his point. Yet that cup sat below a dripping branch, while the other two stayed shallow. The snail moved all three cups into the open and measured again. This time their levels matched, showing that the first cup had given a crooked answer. The finch chose a higher fork, and the next hard rain passed below her finished nest. She thanked the snail for testing the test, not merely trusting its first result. From then on, the orchard birds used several cups before changing their plans.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: Careful observers check whether a measuring method, not just one reading, can be trusted.
An orchard is safe for nests whenever its ground looks dry.
A finch should always choose the highest branch in a tree.
Berry dye allows birds to predict exactly when rain will fall.
questions.explanation: The first cup is distorted by a dripping branch, so the animals repeat the measurement under fairer conditions before acting.

questions.stem: Why does the finch finally choose a higher fork?
choices: She wants the orchard birds to admire her nest.
The repeated cup readings give her a sound reason to expect rising water.
The snail tells her that low branches are difficult to reach.
She sees berry dye stain the bark of the lower fork.
questions.explanation: Once cups in the same open setting agree, the finch treats their result as stronger evidence that water may reach the low fork.

questions.stem: What does “crooked” mean in the phrase “a crooked answer”?
choices: Written in berry dye
Bent into a round shape
Misleading because the test was unfair
Too shallow to be measured
questions.explanation: The cup under the dripping branch reports more water than the cups in the open, so its answer is distorted and misleading.

questions.stem: What caused the first cup to fill unusually quickly?
choices: The finch poured water into it.
The snail placed it in a puddle.
Berry dye attracted extra raindrops.
It was sitting below a dripping branch.
questions.explanation: The passage directly contrasts that cup with the other two and notes that it sat beneath a dripping branch.

lesson.strategy: Track the fable’s two rounds of measurement. Ask what changes when the cups move into the open, then connect the fairer test to the finch’s safer choice.

signals.means: The snail replaces an unsupported disagreement with an observable test.
This turn reveals a flaw that weakens the first apparent result.
Agreement under equal conditions makes the repeated evidence more dependable.

vocab.inContext: holding only a small depth of water
checked the amount by using marked cups
misleading because the setup bent the result

skillTips.main-idea: Connect the flawed first cup, the fair retest, and the protected nest; together they express the fable’s lesson.
skillTips.inference: Use the finch’s changed behavior as evidence: she moves only after the open cups produce matching readings.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read beyond the literal shape of “crooked”; the uneven setup shows that the answer itself is misleading.
skillTips.detail: Keep the two cup locations separate so you can identify exactly what made the first reading unusual.

passages.title: A Belief with Hinges
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
People sometimes imagine a strong belief as a door bolted shut. No doubt can enter, so conviction appears firm. Yet a belief that cannot respond to evidence is not strong in the useful sense; it is merely protected. Inquiry needs beliefs that can bear weight while remaining open to revision.

Consider a bridge inspector who sees a hairline crack. She should not announce that collapse is certain, nor dismiss the mark because certainty is absent. She can form a provisional judgment: the crack matters enough to test. New measurements may show harmless surface wear, or they may reveal a deeper fault. Either result changes what she has reason to believe.

This does not mean changing one’s mind with every rumor. A hinged belief opens for relevant evidence, not for any passing push. Its firmness comes from the quality of its supports and from clear conditions for revision. Intellectual humility therefore differs from indecision. It permits action on the best available reasons while admitting that better reasons may arrive. The point of inquiry is not to avoid commitment forever, but to make commitments capable of learning.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the passage’s main idea?
choices: Strong beliefs should remain unchanged until every possible doubt disappears.
A responsible belief can guide action while remaining open to relevant evidence and revision.
Bridge inspections show that physical measurements are more useful than philosophical thought.
Intellectual humility requires a person to delay every important commitment.
questions.explanation: The door image, inspection example, and conclusion all describe commitment that is supported yet able to learn from better reasons.

questions.stem: Why does the author use the bridge inspector as an example?
choices: To show that visible cracks always predict a bridge collapse
To argue that only trained experts may revise a belief
To show how someone can investigate and act without pretending to possess certainty
To prove that surface wear never deserves attention
questions.explanation: The inspector neither declares collapse nor ignores the crack; she adopts a testable judgment that can change with measurements.

questions.stem: In this passage, what does “revision” most nearly mean?
choices: A rumor repeated by several people
A permanent refusal to choose
A measurement of a physical crack
A reasoned change made in light of new evidence
questions.explanation: The passage says new measurements can alter what the inspector has reason to believe, defining revision as evidence-based change.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what gives a hinged belief its firmness?
choices: The quality of its supports and clear conditions for revision
The number of people who repeat it
The believer’s ability to ignore every doubt
A promise never to alter it
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly says firmness comes from good supports and clear conditions under which the belief may change.

lesson.strategy: Follow the door metaphor through the bridge example. Separate firmness from stubbornness, then identify how evidence can support both action now and revision later.

signals.means: The author challenges the opening picture of strength as being closed to doubt.
This names a conclusion held for now while further testing remains possible.
The author limits the claim so openness is not confused with being easily swayed.

vocab.inContext: a firmly held belief or sense of certainty
accepted for now but open to later change
a reasoned update after new evidence appears

skillTips.main-idea: Combine the hinge metaphor with the final sentence: good commitments are sturdy enough to act on and flexible enough to learn.
skillTips.inference: Ask what the inspector’s middle course avoids; she rejects both unsupported certainty and careless dismissal.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the measurements that may change the judgment to infer that “revision” means an evidence-based update.
skillTips.detail: Return to the third paragraph for the two stated sources of firmness instead of relying only on the door image.

passages.title: When Familiarity Borrows Truth
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Read an unfamiliar claim once, and it may feel awkward. Encounter the same claim several times, and its words become easier to process. That ease can quietly be mistaken for evidence. Psychologists call this pattern the illusory truth effect: repetition may increase a statement’s felt credibility even when repetition adds no support.

The mechanism begins with processing fluency. A familiar sentence takes less mental work to recognize, just as a well-used path is easier to walk. The mind must then interpret that ease. If the source is forgotten, familiarity may be misread as a sign that the claim is widely known or previously verified. A neat rhyme, clear type, or simple wording can also increase fluency, though none can make a false statement true.

The effect is a tendency, not a switch controlling every judgment. Prior knowledge, attention to sources, and an obvious contradiction can all resist it. Repetition can also serve a good claim by helping people remember it, so repetition itself is not proof of deception.

A useful response is to separate recognition from verification. Ask whether a claim feels supported because evidence accompanies it, or merely because its shape is familiar. That pause turns a vague sense of truth into a question that sources can answer.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Repeated statements are usually accurate because many people have checked them.
Simple wording is the main cause of every mistaken belief.
Repetition can make a claim feel credible through familiarity, so recognition should be separated from verification.
People can completely prevent judgment errors by ignoring familiar claims.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how repetition creates fluency, limits the effect, and recommends checking evidence rather than trusting familiarity.

questions.stem: Why does forgetting a claim’s source make familiarity riskier?
choices: A forgotten source makes every sentence harder to read.
People then assume that all repeated claims are deliberate lies.
The mind stops recognizing words that appeared earlier.
A person may retain the feeling of recognition without remembering whether the source was dependable.
questions.explanation: The text says source information may fade while familiarity remains, allowing ease to be misread as prior verification.

questions.stem: What does “fluency” mean in the passage’s discussion of processing?
choices: The ease with which the mind recognizes and processes a statement
The truth of a claim established by independent evidence
The frequency with which a source publishes new material
The ability to remember the exact wording of every claim
questions.explanation: The passage introduces fluency just after saying repeated words become easier to process and compares it with an easy path.

questions.stem: Which factor does the passage say can resist the effect of repetition?
choices: Using a neat rhyme
Paying attention to the claim’s source
Printing the statement in clear type
Making the wording simpler
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names attention to sources, along with prior knowledge and obvious contradiction, as a resisting factor.

lesson.strategy: Trace the chain from repetition to easier processing, then from easier processing to misplaced credibility. Use the limiting paragraph to avoid treating the effect as automatic.

signals.means: The phrase links smoother processing to the mistaken feeling of evidence.
This qualification shows that repetition influences judgment without determining it.
The passage shifts from explaining the effect to a practical way of checking it.

vocab.inContext: the quality of seeming believable or trustworthy
mental ease in recognizing and processing words
checking a claim against supporting evidence

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the psychological mechanism and the recommended check; either half alone leaves the passage’s purpose incomplete.
skillTips.inference: Link lost source memory with remaining familiarity to explain why recognition can outlast knowledge of reliability.
skillTips.vocabulary: The path comparison defines “fluency” through ease, not through correctness or perfect recall.
skillTips.detail: Sort factors into those that increase processing ease and those that help a reader resist mistaking ease for truth.

passages.title: A Clock That Listens to Atoms
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An atomic clock does not count atoms, and its timekeeping does not depend on radioactive decay. It uses a regular transition between energy states inside atoms as a reference. For cesium-133, the official definition of the second is tied to 9,192,631,770 periods of radiation associated with one particular transition.

The practical clock begins with an electronic oscillator that produces microwaves. Cesium atoms pass through or interact with that signal. When the microwave frequency is slightly wrong, fewer atoms make the desired transition. When it is near resonance, the response grows stronger. A feedback system continually adjusts the oscillator toward the atomic response. Electronics count the stabilized cycles and turn them into seconds.

The atoms are therefore a reference, not a tiny display with hands. Real devices must control magnetic fields, motion, collisions, temperature, and electronic noise because these can shift a measurement. Different clock designs reduce different disturbances. Laboratories compare several clocks, estimate uncertainty, and correct for relativity when height or motion matters.

No single instrument silently defines time for the world. National laboratories compare standards, and international organizations combine measurements into shared time scales. Atomic clocks support navigation, telecommunications, power networks, and scientific tests because distant systems can coordinate against a carefully measured rhythm. Their strength comes from a loop: physics supplies a reproducible transition, engineering keeps an oscillator aligned with it, and comparison reveals remaining error.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage’s main idea?
choices: Atomic clocks obtain time by measuring how quickly radioactive cesium disappears.
A cesium atom contains a tiny clock face that directly displays international time.
One laboratory instrument defines world time without comparison or correction.
Atomic clocks steer an electronic oscillator toward a reproducible atomic transition, while controlling and comparing sources of error.
questions.explanation: The passage follows the reference, feedback loop, corrections, and comparisons that make precise timekeeping possible.

questions.stem: Why does the clock need a feedback system?
choices: The electronic oscillator can drift, so the atomic response is used to steer it back toward resonance.
Cesium atoms must be replaced every second after they decay.
Feedback changes the official number of periods in a second.
The system prevents relativity from applying at different heights.
questions.explanation: The response reveals whether the microwave signal is off frequency, allowing repeated adjustment of the oscillator.

questions.stem: What does “resonance” mean in this passage?
choices: The loss of every atomic signal because of noise
The frequency region where the applied microwaves most strongly produce the chosen atomic transition
The comparison of two countries’ legal time zones
The radioactive lifetime of cesium-133
questions.explanation: Near resonance, more atoms make the desired energy transition, providing the response used to tune the oscillator.

questions.stem: What does the passage say laboratories may correct for?
choices: The price of an electronic oscillator
The spelling of the word cesium
Relativity when height or motion matters
The number of time zones in a country
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names relativity alongside uncertainty estimates and controls for physical disturbances.

lesson.strategy: Follow the control loop: oscillator, atoms, measured response, correction, and counted cycles. Keep the physical reference separate from the electronics that display time.

signals.means: This identifies the atomic response used to judge the microwave frequency.
This corrects the image of atoms acting as a complete clock by themselves.

signals.phrase: Their strength comes from a loop
signals.means: This summarizes the partnership among physics, engineering, and comparison.

vocab.inContext: an electronic system that produces a repeating microwave signal
the frequency region that strongly drives the selected atomic transition
a measured bound on how far a clock result may be from the best estimate

skillTips.main-idea: Include the atomic reference, electronic feedback, and ongoing control and comparison of error.
skillTips.inference: Use the stronger or weaker atomic response as information that tells the controller which way to tune.
skillTips.vocabulary: Define resonance from what changes there: the desired atomic transition becomes more likely.
skillTips.detail: Separate named physical corrections from applications such as navigation and telecommunications.

passages.title: The Blue Chalk Test
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Rain left a dark patch on the community room floor. Mei dried it, but she could not see where the water entered. Three windows stood above the patch. Each frame looked tight.

Before the next storm, Mei drew a blue chalk line under every window. She also laid a strip of dry paper on each sill. Then she waited. The rain began after lunch. Two papers stayed crisp. The third grew soft at one corner, and the chalk below it ran in a thin trail.

Mei found a loose seal beside that corner. She pressed it back and asked the caretaker to repair it. During the following storm, all three papers remained dry. The floor stayed clean, and Mei saved the chalk marks in her notebook. Her small test had turned a hidden leak into a clear path.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Mei uses a simple test to trace a hidden leak and confirm that the repair works.
A caretaker teaches Mei how to draw with blue chalk.
Three old windows must be replaced after every storm.
Mei turns the community room into a place for weather notes.
questions.explanation: The paper and chalk identify one wet corner, and the dry papers in the later storm confirm that its seal was the source.

questions.stem: Why does Mei put paper under all three windows?
choices: She plans to cover every sill with paper.
She does not yet know which window allows the water inside.
She wants to compare three kinds of chalk.
The caretaker asks her to clean every frame.
questions.explanation: All three windows stand above the floor patch and look tight, so Mei must test each possible source under the same storm.

questions.stem: What is a “sill” in this story?
choices: A blue mark used for measuring rain
A tool used to press a loose seal
The ledge along the bottom of a window
A wet patch in the middle of a floor
questions.explanation: Mei lays paper on each sill to catch water coming through a window, so the sill is the window’s bottom ledge.

questions.stem: What does Mei find beside the wet corner?
choices: A broken piece of chalk
A hole in the paper strip
A note from the caretaker
A loose window seal
questions.explanation: The story directly says Mei finds a loose seal beside the corner where the paper softens and the chalk runs.

lesson.strategy: Follow Mei’s evidence from the floor patch to three equal tests, one wet corner, and a dry later storm. Each step narrows or confirms the cause.

signals.means: Mei prepares a test before new rain can reveal the leak’s route.
One paper changes while the others stay crisp, isolating the likely source.
A later event checks whether repairing the seal actually solved the problem.

vocab.inContext: the ledge at the bottom of a window
material that closes a gap against water
a thin visible path left by moving water

skillTips.main-idea: Retell the whole problem-solution arc: hidden leak, fair test, repair, and successful check in new rain.
skillTips.inference: Use the three similar windows to explain why Mei cannot test only one before she has evidence.
skillTips.vocabulary: The paper’s location beneath each window helps define “sill” as the lower ledge, not a separate tool.
skillTips.detail: Match each clue to its location: soft paper, running chalk, and the loose seal all appear at one corner.

passages.title: Longitude and the Sea Clock
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For centuries, sailors could estimate how far north or south they were by watching the Sun and stars. Finding longitude, their east-west position, was harder. A navigator needed to compare local noon with the time at a known reference place. Every hour of difference represented part of Earth’s daily turn.

The idea required a clock that kept accurate time during a long voyage. Pendulum clocks worked on land, but a rolling ship and changing temperature disturbed them. In eighteenth-century Britain, carpenter and clockmaker John Harrison spent decades developing sea clocks. He reduced friction, allowed parts to adjust for temperature, and eventually built a watchlike timekeeper that performed well at sea.

Harrison was not the only person studying longitude, and astronomy remained another important method. Yet reliable marine timekeepers gave navigators a practical new tool. By carrying reference time across the ocean, a clock could help turn two observations into a position on a chart.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Sailors abandoned astronomy as soon as accurate land clocks appeared.
Reliable sea clocks helped navigators find longitude by preserving a reference time during voyages.
John Harrison discovered that Earth completes its daily turn once each hour.
Pendulum clocks became more accurate when placed on rolling ships.
questions.explanation: The passage connects the longitude problem with Harrison’s durable timekeepers and the comparison of local noon to reference time.

questions.stem: Why could a difference between local and reference time reveal longitude?
choices: Stars appear only when a ship reaches the correct longitude.
A ship’s clock moves faster when it travels west.
Different east-west positions reach local noon at different points in Earth’s turn.
Longitude is the distance a pendulum swings during one hour.
questions.explanation: Because Earth turns, local noon occurs at different times from place to place; comparing those times indicates east-west separation.

questions.stem: What does “friction” mean in the clockmaker’s work?
choices: The study of the Sun and stars
A ship’s east-west position
A written time kept at a reference place
Resistance produced when moving parts rub against one another
questions.explanation: Harrison reduced friction while improving a mechanism, so the word refers to resistance between the clock’s moving surfaces.

questions.stem: What two conditions disturbed pendulum clocks at sea?
choices: A rolling ship and changing temperature
Clouds and a lack of charts
Salt water and missing stars
Local noon and reference time
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly identifies a ship’s rolling motion and temperature changes as problems for pendulum clocks.

lesson.strategy: Build the historical chain: longitude needed a time comparison, voyages disturbed old clocks, and Harrison improved timekeepers that could carry the needed reference.

signals.means: This contrast introduces the unsolved east-west navigation problem.
The phrase identifies the practical condition that a time-based solution needed.
This turn acknowledges other methods before stating the clocks’ importance.

vocab.inContext: a location measured east or west
a known standard used for comparison
resistance between parts that rub as they move

skillTips.main-idea: Link the navigation need to the invention’s function; Harrison matters here because his clocks preserved comparison time at sea.
skillTips.inference: Combine Earth’s daily turn with different local noons to reason from a time gap to an east-west position.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use Harrison’s effort to reduce a mechanical problem to infer that “friction” occurs where clock parts rub.
skillTips.detail: Look in the land-versus-sea contrast for the two exact conditions that made pendulum clocks unreliable aboard ships.

passages.title: A Compass Above the Dunes
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A dung beetle that has shaped a ball of food needs to leave a crowded pile quickly. Other beetles may steal the ball, so wandering in circles is costly. Some ball-rolling dung beetles climb onto their prize, turn in place, and then push it away along a fairly straight route. Their useful compass is overhead.

By day, the Sun can provide a strong direction cue. Even when the Sun is partly hidden, patterns of polarized light across the sky can help some insects maintain a bearing. At night, certain dung beetles can use the broad glow of the Milky Way. This does not mean they read individual constellations as a person might. Instead, the uneven band of light gives them a large-scale orientation cue.

Researchers have tested these abilities by changing what beetles can see. In controlled arenas, small caps can block a beetle’s view upward, while projected skies can offer selected celestial patterns. Routes become less direct when useful sky cues disappear. Such experiments do not tell us what the journey feels like to a beetle. They do show that a small traveler can extract direction from light spread across an immense sky.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Dung beetles travel mainly by following the scent of other beetles.
The Milky Way is made of individual lights that insects can name.
Some dung beetles use broad patterns of celestial light to keep their food-moving routes straight.
Controlled arenas teach dung beetles to make larger balls of food.
questions.explanation: The passage describes daytime and nighttime sky cues, then explains experiments showing less direct routes when those cues vanish.

questions.stem: Why is a fairly straight route valuable to a ball-rolling beetle?
choices: It helps the beetle identify individual constellations.
It makes polarized light brighter at night.
It allows the beetle to return its food to the crowded pile.
It helps the beetle leave competitors quickly without wasting effort in circles.
questions.explanation: The opening says other beetles may steal the food and that circular wandering is costly, making direct escape advantageous.

questions.stem: In this passage, what is a “bearing”?
choices: A direction of travel that can be maintained
A container used to protect a food ball
A bright star within a constellation
A circle marked on the floor of an arena
questions.explanation: Polarized light helps insects maintain a bearing as they travel, so bearing means a chosen direction rather than an object.

questions.stem: What can researchers use to block a beetle’s view upward?
choices: Food balls
Small caps
Polarized maps
Projected dunes
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that small caps can block the beetles’ upward view during controlled tests.

lesson.strategy: Separate observation from experiment: first note the straight route and possible sky cues, then see how removing or selecting those cues changes the route.

signals.means: The passage begins distinguishing the celestial cues available in daylight.
The explanation shifts to a different source of broad light after sunset.
The conclusion states both what the tests support and what they cannot reveal.

vocab.inContext: a steady direction followed during travel
the process of finding and keeping direction
relating to the sky and objects seen there

skillTips.main-idea: Unite the beetle’s problem, the sky cues, and the changed routes in experiments; all three support the central explanation.
skillTips.inference: Use the threat of theft and the cost of circles to explain why direct travel benefits a beetle with a food ball.
skillTips.vocabulary: Nearby words “maintain” and “direction cue” show that a “bearing” is a direction kept during movement.
skillTips.detail: The testing paragraph names two experimental tools; distinguish the hats that remove view from skies that supply patterns.
